items.title: Wayfinder: Rebuild Fond as an API-first life operating platform
items.body:
## Destination

An implementation-ready master plan for rebuilding Fond as a local-first, multitenant API/CLI platform covering the complete nourishment, health, fitness, finance, commerce, and investment capability set. The map is complete when focused implementation sessions can proceed without unresolved material product, domain, architecture, safety, provider, testing, or sequencing decisions.

## Notes

Domain: a self-hosted-first life and household operating service that can later support independently managed installations or a Fond-managed service.

Every session must use the Wayfinder and grilling skills; also use domain-modeling when that skill becomes available. This map plans decisions and does not implement product capabilities.

Standing constraints confirmed while charting:

- Remove the current product UI and preserve none of its design decisions. A minimal native shell may support Apple Health authorization/sync and meal-photo capture as infrastructure for the eventual native client.
- Treat all existing code, contracts, schemas, and tests as replaceable evidence; the project is pre-production and has no compatibility or data-migration obligations.
- Organize a TypeScript/Effect monorepo as a modular monolith with strict domain boundaries. The independently deployed DGX model runtime is accessed through a typed provider interface.
- Use PostgreSQL as the authoritative store and S3-compatible storage for larger artifacts. SQLite is non-authoritative.
- Make the self-hosted deployment the data-sovereignty default. External providers receive only explicitly permitted minimum data; remote AI is opt-in.
- A household is a tenant. Shared household resources and private member data have distinct ownership; adults do not implicitly gain access to one another's private records.
- Models propose structured candidates; deterministic domain code validates invariants and owns calculations. Provenance, corrections, model/provider versions, and confidence are platform-wide concerns.
- Begin irreversible external actions with explicit human approval, while leaving room for future policy-bounded autonomy with limits, revocation, and auditability.
- Expose a versioned JSON/HTTP API with generated OpenAPI and a thin CLI using the same public contracts. Long-running operations are jobs; mutations are idempotent.
- Treat pure domain, contract, real-database integration, provider conformance, public API/CLI end-to-end, and deterministic model-fixture tests as acceptance gates.
- Deliver the nourishment loop first, then health, fitness, finance/commerce, and investments. Self-hosting must remain portable toward horizontally scalable managed operation.

## Decisions so far

<!-- Resolved decisions are indexed here by their ticket names. -->

- [Define Fond bounded contexts and dependency rules](https://github.com/eggdev/fond/issues/11) — Fixed the long-term capability ownership map while requiring strict data ownership, consumer-owned cross-domain ports, and just-in-time deep module seams.
- [Research Apple Health ingestion constraints for API-first Fond](https://github.com/eggdev/fond/issues/24) — Established that HealthKit requires a signed native bridge with per-type anchored capture and a durable device outbox; server-only ingestion is not possible.
- [Research household purchase ingestion across Costco, Instacart, and Amazon](https://github.com/eggdev/fond/issues/25) — Selected a provider-neutral receipt and artifact import baseline because supported consumer purchase-history automation is largely unavailable.
- [Research Plaid and Alpaca capabilities and safety controls](https://github.com/eggdev/fond/issues/26) — Separated Plaid read-side synchronization from approval-bound Alpaca trading with durable reconciliation, scoped grants, limits, and kill switches.
- [Decide the clean-slate repository reset and monorepo topology](https://github.com/eggdev/fond/issues/12) — Chose an atomic legacy reset and a Bun workspace whose activated contexts are alias-addressed deep modules, promoted to packages only under demonstrated pressure and protected by automated dependency rules.
- [Define household identity, membership, ownership, and consent](https://github.com/eggdev/fond/issues/13) — Split installation-level accounts from household memberships with stewards, explicit guardian links, per-domain ownership defaults, and revocable category-level consent grants; all dependent features are modeled now and implemented later.
- [Define authentication and tenant-isolation architecture](https://github.com/eggdev/fond/issues/14) — Adopted an Authenticator port with a Tailscale whois mode first and deferred Better Auth, explicit per-request household context, use-case-level authorization with ActorContext, and owner-column scoping backed by RLS in one shared schema.
- [Define provenance, correction, audit, and derived-state semantics](https://github.com/eggdev/fond/issues/15) — Made observations immutable with source-keyed dedup, supersession chains, inferential-only confidence, an in-transaction audit log, and compute-on-read projections.
- [Define API resources, jobs, errors, versioning, and idempotency](https://github.com/eggdev/fond/issues/16) — Made a single Effect HttpApi tree the source of truth for the server, OpenAPI, and CLI, with household path segments, a mutable pre-GA v1, RFC 9457 typed errors that hide cross-tenant existence, provider-boundary jobs polled to completion, natural-key-first idempotency, cursor-only collections, and a CLI that adds formatting alone.
- [Define persistence, object storage, migrations, backup, and restore](https://github.com/eggdev/fond/issues/17) — Chose `@effect/sql-pg` with hand-written DDL over a schema-per-context PostgreSQL database, a two-table foreign-key spine, transaction-scoped row-level security backed by one shared consent function, presigned S3-compatible artifact upload with an explicit commit, and point-in-time recovery proven by an executable restore drill.

## Not yet specified

- The domain-specific evidence and policy inputs used by cross-domain Guidance for nutrition, health, fitness, recovery, and family recommendations. The shared Guidance model is now ticketed, but its concrete recommendation families depend on the owning domain contracts.
- Workout generation, progression, and recovery adaptation beyond the base Fitness catalogue and training-record semantics. Their split between deterministic programming, Guidance, and model proposals depends on the shared Guidance decision.
- Live job progress over Server-Sent Events, layered additively on the polled job resource. It graduates when the native shell needs streaming meal-photo inference progress and the model-provider decision has fixed what progress events contain.
- The exact staged implementation roadmap after the first vertical slice; later slices will graduate as earlier domain decisions clear the fog.

## Out of scope

- Product UI, visual design, dashboards, and general mobile/desktop interaction until the named API capabilities are complete; only the minimal Apple Health and photo-capture native shell is permitted.
- Preservation of the current UI, Swift application architecture, API compatibility, or existing database migrations.
- Building or operating the DGX model runtime itself; Fond defines and consumes its provider contract.
- Pricing, billing, sales, and commercial operation of a future managed service.
- Unbounded autonomous control of external accounts during the initial platform build; any later autonomy requires explicit policy, limits, revocation, and auditability.

items.title: Per-tenant Greptime trace tables with tenant-level TTLs and no default partitioning
items.body:
Today we write traces into a shared Greptime table, `opentelemetry_traces`, and read them back from that same table in the API. We want to move to one trace table per tenant so retention can be configured per tenant/table instead of globally.

Greptime supports overriding the target trace table via the `X-Greptime-Trace-Table-Name` header, and its default trace table model applies a 16-way `trace_id` partition rule. That default is fine for a small number of shared trace tables, but it does not scale if we create one table per tenant. With tenant tables, default partitioning would multiply into too many partitions overall, so partitioning should no longer be the default.

We can keep partitioned tenant trace tables as a future/pro-tier option with migration via the repartition feature.

**Required changes**
- Introduce one Greptime traces table per tenant, with a stable naming convention derived from tenant/organization ID.
- Provision tenant tables explicitly with the Greptime trace data model and tenant-specific TTL.
- Stop relying on Greptime’s default trace-table creation shape for tenant tables, since that shape includes default `trace_id` partitioning.
- Update trace ingestion so writes are routed to the tenant’s table instead of always landing in shared `opentelemetry_traces`.
- Update the trace read path in the API to resolve the tenant table dynamically instead of hard-coding `opentelemetry_traces`.
- Update schema introspection and caching in the trace service so it is table-aware rather than assuming a single shared table.
- Cache discovered `metadataColumns` and optional trace column presence per tenant table in [service.ts](/Users/h/Documents/hebo-platform/apps/api/src/modules/traces/service.ts), instead of using one global cache entry. This avoids repeated `information_schema.columns` lookups while keeping trace queries correct for each tenant table.
- Define fallback behavior for spans that do not have tenant context. Either:
  - keep them in a shared non-tenant table, or
  - scope this change to gateway gen-AI traces only.

**Conceptual OTLP exporter change**
The current exporter setup is effectively process-wide and uses static headers. To support multiple tables, replace the single trace exporter with a tenant-aware exporter/multiplexer:

- Resolve the tenant from span attributes already attached during request handling, e.g. `hebo.organization.id`.
- Map tenant ID to a Greptime table name.
- Group exported spans by resolved table name.
- For each table group, send the batch with the normal Greptime trace pipeline header plus `X-Greptime-Trace-Table-Name: <tenant_table>`.
- Cache delegate exporters/clients per table so we do not recreate an exporter on every batch.
- Keep table provisioning separate from normal export flow so TTL and table options are controlled explicitly, rather than depending on first-write auto-creation.

**Non-goals**
- No migration or backfill of existing traces.
- No partitioning by default for tenant tables.
- No UI change expected in console; this should remain an API/storage concern.

**Acceptance criteria**
- New traces for a tenant are written to that tenant’s own Greptime trace table.
- Each tenant table can have its own TTL.
- Tenant trace tables are created without default `trace_id` partitioning.
- API trace list/detail queries work against the correct tenant table.
- Trace schema discovery is cached per tenant table rather than globally.
- There is no migration/backfill requirement for existing shared-table traces.
- Partitioned tenant trace tables, if supported later, are explicitly opt-in rather than the default.

**References**
- Greptime OTLP traces docs: https://docs.greptime.com/user-guide/ingest-data/for-observability/opentelemetry/
- Greptime trace data model docs: https://docs.greptime.com/user-guide/traces/data-model/
- Greptime manage data docs: https://docs.greptime.com/user-guide/manage-data/overview/#manage-data-retention-with-ttl-policies
- Greptime repartition docs: https://docs.greptime.com/user-guide/deployments-administration/manage-data/repartition/

items.title: Unified model+entity log — fold schema extensions into entity data tables as special entries
items.body:
## Background

Surfaced during Data-Ingestion QA Sub-project B brainstorm (2026-04-22).

Today the schema-extension log and the entity data log are separate:
- Model schema lives in its own extension log (append-only, folded on read; Sub-project B adds savepoints every N extensions).
- Entity data lives in its own per-tenant/per-model tables.

These two logs are causally related — a model's schema governs what entities can be written, and new entities can trigger schema extensions. But they're stored, indexed, and queried separately. That creates a few observable frictions:

- **No unified transactional consistency** — a schema extension and the entity write that triggered it commit via separate paths. A storage backend's atomic primitive can't span both unless we explicitly orchestrate it.
- **No unified audit surface** — \"show me everything that happened at time T\" requires querying two logs and merging.
- **No unified bi-temporal query path** — \"as-at T, what was the model and what entities existed?\" is two queries with independent temporal consistency.

## Proposal

Consider folding the schema extension log into the entity data tables as a distinguished entry kind. One append-only event stream per tenant (or per model), where each event is either:

- `SchemaExtension { delta: SchemaDelta, level: ChangeLevel, ... }`
- `EntityWrite { entityID, state, data: ModelNode, ... }`
- `Savepoint { snapshot: ModelNode, ... }` — continues to work the same way, bounds fold cost for both schema and entities.

Benefits if it pans out:
- **Single transactional commit** — a write that causes a schema extension commits atomically with the entity write.
- **Single audit stream** — one query returns all writes at time T across both concerns.
- **Unified bi-temporal query semantics** — as-at-T becomes a single reverse-scan against one log.
- **Simpler cross-plugin contract** — one \"append event, atomically\" primitive per backend, replacing today's separate schema-extension and entity-write code paths.

## Risks / open questions

- **Schema and entity writes have very different cardinality.** Schema extensions are rare; entity writes are the hot path. Storing them in the same table might hurt entity write latency if the indexing strategy isn't careful.
- **Per-model vs per-tenant partition.** The right partition key is non-obvious — per-model gives schema-local causal order but loses tenant-wide \"at time T\" queries.
- **Migration from the current split design is non-trivial.** Existing deployments have separate log tables; consolidation requires a data migration per backend.
- **Does this actually buy us anything that orchestration at the service layer can't provide?** If the service layer can commit schema + entity writes within a shared transaction scope (backend-specific), the unified-log benefit is mostly audit/query ergonomics rather than correctness.

## Scope

Feature request only — design decision, not a task. If we pursue this it's its own initiative with its own design cycle.

## Acceptance criteria for closing this issue (not for implementing it)

- [ ] A design spec under \`docs/superpowers/specs/\` evaluating the proposal, or an explicit decision to not pursue it (with rationale).

## References

- Brainstorm context: Data-Ingestion QA Sub-project B design doc (forthcoming).
- Parent initiative: Data-Ingestion QA overview, \`docs/superpowers/specs/2026-04-21-data-ingestion-qa-overview.md\`.
- Related tracking: #86 (unbound-data ingestion — different feature, similar theme of \"how data and schema interact\").

Source task file: `tasks/03-data-operations.md`

### T14: Dataset Catalog and Current File Lineage

Dependencies: T07, T13.

Product goal:

Let analysts and downstream workflows refer to tenant-owned analytical datasets by stable catalog entries, current source file metadata, processing readiness, quality status, and lineage.

Implementation notes:

- A dataset represents the business asset, such as `Meter readings - 2026`.
- Full dataset version history is deferred per `docs/data-model.md`; the first implementation tracks the current uploaded file, processing readiness, quality summary, deprecation state, and lineage directly on the dataset.
- Evaluation inputs should reference datasets plus the quality report and ingestion job that made them ready.
- Deprecated datasets remain visible for history but should not be selected by default for new evaluations.
- Dataset status vocabulary must align with shared contracts and UI badges.

Deliver:

- Dataset schema/repositories aligned with `docs/data-model.md`, including `file_object_id`, dataset type, processing status, quality status, schema fingerprint, record counts, `ready_at`, and `deprecated_at`.
- Dataset create, list, detail, patch, deprecate, and restore endpoints.
- Lineage links to file object, uploader, ingestion job, latest quality report, current readiness, and downstream evaluations when available.
- Filters for dataset type, processing status, quality status, deprecation state, and search.

Acceptance criteria:

- Registering `Meter readings - 2026` from an uploaded file creates one dataset record linked to its file object and an initial ingestion job.
- Catalog filters can return only `dataset_type=meter_readings` and `processing_status=completed` or equivalent ready status.
- Dataset detail exposes current source file metadata, uploader, processing status, quality status, record counts, schema fingerprint, and linked quality report.
- Deprecated `Meter readings - 2025` remains visible with a Deprecated badge and is excluded from default new-evaluation input selection.
- A user from Cascade cannot list, open, patch, deprecate, or restore Northwind datasets.
- Tests document that full replacement/version history is deferred rather than partially implemented.

type.name: Feature
type.description: A request, idea, or new functionality

items.body: acme-auditlog-service is the centralized audit trail for the Acme platform, built with .NET 8. It receives authenticated audit events from other services — such as acme-tickets-service, acme-auth-service, acme-files-service, and acme-notifications — and stores them in an append-only fashion so actions can be traced by tenant, user, or resource. It uses the shared event and error schemas defined in acme-contracts, and it enforces multi-tenant isolation by reading tenant_id from JWTs issued by acme-auth-service. The service exposes a query endpoint for admins to review activity. Responses are returned in the standardized problem+json format. Tests include unit tests for the event model and integration tests for the audit ingestion endpoint.

items.title: New Featues Routes
items.body:
### Architectural Instruction for Cloud & Web App Teams **Target Systems:** `backend.aryorithm.com` (API), `app.aryorithm.com` (`./dashboard`), and `hub.aryorithm.com` **Scope:** Implementing Universal 7-Artifact Management, Forking, Public/Private Sovereign Isolation, and Granular Workspace Sharing. --- ### 1. Architectural Baseline & The 7 Artifact Classes The backend currently manages 7 distinct artifact classes across multiple disparate routers (`hub_assets.py`, `hub.py`, `blueprints.py`, `modelvault.py`): 1. **`package` (`.spkg`)** — In-kernel eBPF filters, reflex gates, honeytap vaccines. 2. **`dataset` (`.slab`)** — Binary sensor matrices (`0x534C4142`) for training and micro-benchmarking. 3. **`model` (`.onnx`)** — INT8 post-training quantized models for `libxinfer.so`. 4. **`pcap` (`.pcap`)** — OT/IT network captures and attack replays. 5. **`scenario` (`.tar.gz`)** — Cyber-range Purdue digital twin topologies for `sentinel-matrix`. 6. **`blueprint` (`.blueprint` / `model_routes.yaml`)** — Physical hardware bindings and ModelRouter DAG configurations. 7. **`appliance` (`.aryopack`)** — Self-extracting edge host installation images. To support user workspaces, forking, visibility switching, and sharing, the API must unify these 7 types under a standardized resource and authorization model. --- ### 2. Routes That Must Change | Existing Route | Current Behavior | Required Modification | Rationale | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | `POST /api/v1/hub/publish` | Accepts `package\|pcap\|dataset\|model\|scenario`. Always writes to the public registry. | **1.** Expand `asset_type` to accept all 7 types: `package`, `pcap`, `dataset`, `model`, `scenario`, `blueprint`, `appliance` (restricting `appliance` to `super_admin`).
**2.** Add multipart field `visibility: "public" \| "private"` (defaults to `private`).
**3.** Automatically bind the uploaded artifact to the caller’s `tenant_id` and `user_id` from the JWT. | Unifies upload ingestion into a single entrypoint while enabling private-by-default uploads from `./dashboard`. | | `GET /api/v1/hub/catalog` | Public-only read model returning assets from the 5 legacy catalogs. | **1.** Include `blueprint` and `appliance` in results.
**2.** Add auth awareness: If unauthenticated, return only `visibility="public"`. If authenticated via JWT, return `public` assets **plus** `private` assets belonging to the caller's tenant or explicitly shared with the caller.
**3.** Add query filter: `?scope=all\|public\|private\|shared`. | Allows `./dashboard` to display both public marketplace items and the user's private library in a single search view. | | `GET /api/v1/hub/search` | Full-text fuzzy search across public items only. | Same scoping changes as `GET /hub/catalog`: filter query by tenant ownership and visibility parameters (`?scope=`). | Ensures private SCADA captures and proprietary plant blueprints do not leak into public search results. | | `GET /api/v1/hub/assets/{asset_type}/{slug}` | Returns public metadata; returns `404` if unlisted. | **Authorization check:**
• If `visibility == "public"`, allow access.
• If `visibility == "private"`, verify caller's JWT is within the owning tenant or has an active share record; return `403 Forbidden` (or `404`) if unauthorized.
**Payload expansion:** Include `visibility`, `owner_user_id`, `owner_tenant_id`, `forked_from`, `fork_count`, and `permissions` in the response envelope. | Prevents unauthorized tenant access while providing the frontend with user capability flags (`can_edit`, `can_fork`, `can_share`). | | `DELETE /api/v1/hub/assets/{asset_type}/{slug}` | Deletes developer asset or yanks authority asset. | Validate ownership: Only the asset owner, tenant admin, or `super_admin` can delete. If the asset has active downstream forks, mark as `orphaned_root` rather than deleting underlying storage files. | Prevents deletion of a parent artifact from breaking user forks. | | `GET /api/v1/blueprints` | Tenant-scoped visual blueprints only (JSON graphs). | Add link to compiled `.blueprint` binary artifact in `hub_assets` and expose `visibility` status. | Connects visual diagram drafts in `./dashboard` to published edge blueprints on `hub`. | --- ### 3. New Routes to Implement The web team must implement four new route groups under `/api/v1`: #### Group A: Personal & Tenant Workspace Management (`/api/v1/workspace`) Dedicated endpoints for `app.aryorithm.com` (`./dashboard`) to manage the user’s own artifacts across all 7 types: ``` GET /api/v1/workspace/artifacts POST /api/v1/workspace/artifacts/upload GET /api/v1/workspace/artifacts/{asset_type}/{slug} PATCH /api/v1/workspace/artifacts/{asset_type}/{slug} DELETE /api/v1/workspace/artifacts/{asset_type}/{slug} ``` * **`GET /api/v1/workspace/artifacts`**: * **Auth:** User JWT. * **Query Params:** `?type=all|package|dataset|model|pcap|scenario|blueprint|appliance&visibility=all|public|private|shared&q=&page=1&limit=20`. * **Response:** Returns only artifacts owned by the user's tenant or shared directly with the user. * **`PATCH /api/v1/workspace/artifacts/{asset_type}/{slug}`**: * **Auth:** Admin or Artifact Owner. * **Request Body:** `{ "title"?, "short_description"?, "tags"?, "target_protocols"? }`. * **Response:** Updated metadata. --- #### Group B: Forking Engine (`/api/v1/hub/assets/.../fork`) Allows users to clone any public or shared artifact into their tenant workspace: ``` POST /api/v1/hub/assets/{asset_type}/{slug}/fork GET /api/v1/hub/assets/{asset_type}/{slug}/forks GET /api/v1/hub/assets/{asset_type}/{slug}/lineage ``` * **`POST /api/v1/hub/assets/{asset_type}/{slug}/fork`**: * **Auth:** User JWT. * **Request Body:** `{ "new_slug"?, "title"?, "description"?, "visibility": "private" | "public" }`. * **Behavior:** 1. Validates caller has `VIEW` access to source asset. 2. Clones the metadata record into the caller's tenant. 3. Uses Copy-on-Write (CoW) or hard-links the underlying storage artifact (`.spkg`, `.onnx`, `.slab`, etc.) to prevent storage duplication until modified. 4. Records `forked_from = { asset_type, slug, version, commit_sha256 }`. 5. Increments `fork_count` on the parent asset. * **Response:** `201 Created` with the newly created child artifact envelope. * **`GET /api/v1/hub/assets/{asset_type}/{slug}/lineage`**: * **Auth:** Public for public assets; User JWT for private/shared. * **Response:** Returns parent-child graph (Upstream root $\to$ current artifact $\to$ child forks). --- #### Group C: Sovereign Visibility Switching (`/visibility`) Allows toggling between private tenant isolation and public marketplace visibility: ``` PUT /api/v1/hub/assets/{asset_type}/{slug}/visibility ``` * **`PUT /api/v1/hub/assets/{asset_type}/{slug}/visibility`**: * **Auth:** Tenant Admin or Asset Owner. * **Request Body:** `{ "visibility": "public" | "private", "confirm_sanitized": boolean }`. * **Pre-Flight Validation (when switching to `"public"`):** 1. If `asset_type == "pcap"`: Verify PCAP does not contain RFC 1918 private IP addresses or unencrypted passwords, OR require `confirm_sanitized: true`. 2. If `asset_type == "blueprint"`: Validate that internal hostnames/physical NIC names are scrubbed. * **Behavior:** * `public`: Asset immediately indexes on `hub.aryorithm.com` and global search. * `private`: Asset drops from `hub.aryorithm.com`, visible only in `app.aryorithm.com` for permitted users. * **Response:** `200 OK` `{ "asset_type", "slug", "visibility", "published_to_hub_at" }`. --- #### Group D: Granular Collaboration & Sharing (Google Drive Model) Enables secure sharing of private artifacts with specific users, tenants, or via time-limited access links: ``` GET /api/v1/hub/assets/{asset_type}/{slug}/shares POST /api/v1/hub/assets/{asset_type}/{slug}/shares DELETE /api/v1/hub/assets/{asset_type}/{slug}/shares/{share_id} POST /api/v1/hub/assets/{asset_type}/{slug}/share-links GET /api/v1/hub/shares/received ``` * **`GET /api/v1/hub/assets/{asset_type}/{slug}/shares`**: * **Auth:** Owner or Admin. * **Response:** List of users/tenants granted access and their permission levels. * **`POST /api/v1/hub/assets/{asset_type}/{slug}/shares`**: * **Auth:** Owner or Admin. * **Request Body:** ```json { "grantee_type": "user" | "tenant" | "email", "grantee_id": "usr_abc123" | "tenant_xyz", "permission": "VIEW" | "FORK" | "DEPLOY" | "ADMIN", "expires_at": "2026-12-31T23:59:59Z" | null } ``` * **Permission Semantics:** * `VIEW`: Can inspect metadata, download files, view reports. * `FORK`: Can clone into their own workspace/tenant. * `DEPLOY`: Can push directly to edge appliances via `sentinel-nexus`. * `ADMIN`: Can modify sharing permissions and metadata. * **Response:** `201 Created` with share record. * **`POST /api/v1/hub/assets/{asset_type}/{slug}/share-links`**: * **Auth:** Owner or Admin. * **Request Body:** `{ "permission": "VIEW" | "FORK", "expires_in_hours": 72, "max_uses": 5 }`. * **Response:** `201 Created` with signed, single-use or time-bounded secret link: `https://app.aryorithm.com/share/art_live_secureToken123`. * **`GET /api/v1/hub/shares/received`**: * **Auth:** User JWT. * **Response:** List of all external artifacts shared with the caller or caller’s tenant ("Shared with me" tab). --- ### 4. Database Schema Directives for the Backend Team The backend team must add or migrate the following tables/columns: 1. **Alter `hub_asset_meta` (or create if abstracting over individual tables):** * `tenant_id` (`VARCHAR(64)`, indexed, nullable for system authority assets). * `owner_user_id` (`VARCHAR(64)`, indexed). * `visibility` (`ENUM('public', 'private')`, default `'private'`). * `forked_from_type` (`VARCHAR(32)`, nullable). * `forked_from_slug` (`VARCHAR(128)`, nullable). * `forked_from_version` (`VARCHAR(32)`, nullable). * `fork_count` (`INT`, default `0`). 2. **New Table: `hub_asset_shares`:** * `id` (`VARCHAR(64)`, Primary Key). * `asset_type` (`VARCHAR(32)`, indexed). * `asset_slug` (`VARCHAR(128)`, indexed). * `granter_user_id` (`VARCHAR(64)`). * `grantee_type` (`ENUM('user', 'tenant')`). * `grantee_id` (`VARCHAR(64)`, indexed). * `permission` (`ENUM('VIEW', 'FORK', 'DEPLOY', 'ADMIN')`). * `created_at` (`TIMESTAMP`). * `expires_at` (`TIMESTAMP`, nullable). 3. **New Table: `hub_share_links`:** * `id` (`VARCHAR(64)`, Primary Key). * `token_hash` (`VARCHAR(64)`, Unique Index). * `asset_type` (`VARCHAR(32)`). * `asset_slug` (`VARCHAR(128)`). * `permission` (`ENUM('VIEW', 'FORK')`). * `uses_count` (`INT`, default `0`). * `max_uses` (`INT`, nullable). * `expires_at` (`TIMESTAMP`). --- ### 5. Web Application Frontend Instructions (`./dashboard`) Instruct the frontend team to implement the following user flows: 1. **Universal 7-Artifact Explorer (`app.aryorithm.com/artifacts`):** * Filter tabs: `All Types`, `Packages (.spkg)`, `Datasets (.slab)`, `Models (.onnx)`, `PCAPs (.pcap)`, `Scenarios (.tar.gz)`, `Blueprints (.blueprint)`, `Appliances (.aryopack)`. * Scope toggles: `My Workspace`, `Shared with Me`, `Public Hub`. 2. **Action Toolbar on Artifact Details:** * **Fork Button:** Opens a modal allowing the user to select the destination tenant, adjust the slug, and choose visibility. * **Share Button (Google Drive Style):** * Modal with user search auto-complete. * Permission dropdown (`Viewer`, `Forker`, `Edge Deployer`). * "Generate Expiring Link" tab for third-party forensic auditors. * **Visibility Toggle:** Switch between `Private (Tenant)` and `Public (hub.aryorithm.com)` with an automated confirmation warning on data sanitization. 3. **Lineage Tab:** * On any forked asset, display a breadcrumb banner: *"Forked from `upstream-author/modbus-firewall:v1.2`"*. * If the upstream version changes, show an active badge: *"Upstream update available"*. --- ### 6. Execution Verification Protocol for Web Team The web team must verify implementation using this deterministic sequence: ```bash # 1. Run full backend regression suite to ensure zero breaking changes cd backend .venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/ -q # 2. Add and execute dedicated tests covering the new capabilities: # - tests/test_workspace_artifacts.py (CRUD across all 7 types) # - tests/test_artifact_forking.py (Fork lineage, CoW storage verification) # - tests/test_artifact_visibility.py (Public vs Private isolation assertions) # - tests/test_artifact_sharing.py (RBAC: VIEW vs FORK vs DEPLOY permissions) .venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/test_artifact_*.py -v ``` This instruction provides the complete specification required by the web application and backend teams to implement the feature set while preserving backwards compatibility and strict air-gapped sovereign isolation.

items.title: Shared source architecture: Go server and Colony management API and media proxy
items.body:
## Decision and intended outcome

**Keep provider connectors and credentials in the shared Go ingestion system. The standalone Go source server and Colony expose the same source-management contract and authenticated media-delivery protocol, backed by their own runtimes. Antfly consumes version-bound media references through its generic HTTP content-fetching pipeline.**

Applications should register connections and sources, start/inspect synchronization, and reuse listing, acquisition, publication, ownership and deletion tracking without implementing their own ingestion engine or application-owned `/files` proxy.

This replaces the previous native-fetch-connections/Drive proposal throughout this issue:

- Native Drive, Gmail, Discord and Slack integrations in Antfly are **not prerequisites**.
- Source definitions, ingestion runs and scheduling remain in the Go server or Colony, not the Antfly database server.
- The managed Go/Colony proxy is the intended delivery path, not a temporary workaround that must be replaced by native provider fetching.
- Durable staging (persisting a separate copy of provider bytes before publication) is an optional future delivery mode, **not a requirement**.
- Existing native S3/GCS functionality remains useful; it need not be removed or extended into a universal provider system.

The source catalog stored in Antfly is publication/discovery metadata. It does not transfer ownership of ingestion jobs, provider grants or scheduling to the database.

## Original requirements and agreed interpretation

Numbers refer to the originating `FEATURE_REQUESTS.md`, not GitHub issues. The motivating application used Antfly v0.3.0-rc.9.

| Request | Desired result in this design |
| --- | --- |
| **8. Publish explicit media** | Reuse listing/diff/ownership to publish an explicit media row with provider provenance, selected representation/version, MIME, exact byte length and verified original-byte digest. Its processing reference points to the managed media endpoint. Do not manufacture extracted text. |
| **9. Runtime named credentials; no application file proxy** | Register, rotate and revoke provider connections through the ingestion runtime. Go or Colony resolves protected grants and serves authorized media to Antfly. No app-owned `/files` endpoint or provider credential edits in Antfly startup configuration. |
| **14. Metadata-only docsaf listing** | List provider IDs/keys, versions, sizes and available metadata without downloading or exporting bodies. Content hashing/acquisition is a separate phase. |
| **13. Non-Go applications** | Generated TypeScript/Python/Rust clients use the common management API on either runtime without reimplementing ingestion. |

**Requirement clarification:** the original wording of #9 requested named fetch credentials inside Antfly, including native Drive fetching. The agreed design satisfies the application need using runtime-managed connections in Go/Colony instead. It does **not** claim direct native Drive fetching or a new native provider-connection API implements that wording.

Other model-budget, extraction-quality, retry, media-pass, composed-query and transcriber requests remain separate. Finishing this architecture does not itself qualify every media/model combination.

## Existing PRs and reusable foundations

- [Antfly #1487](https://github.com/antflydb/antfly/pull/1487), previously reviewed at `c0ef17a66939ae4f6feb5a8eaa18417256bef769`.
- [Colony #927](https://github.com/antflydb/colony/pull/927), previously reviewed at `4db4b52bb66d075cdac527b8460f9577a7c040ed` (repository access required).

Those revisions contain useful media/listing/streaming work and shared acquisition/reconciliation machinery. At those reviewed revisions:

- The standalone Go source service exposes its own management listener and signed media URLs. It persists control/checkpoint/verification metadata; its proxy obtains bytes from the provider on reads. This is not durable staging of complete file bodies.
- Its management routes use `/v1/profile`, `/v1/connections/...`, `/v1/sources/...`, `/v1/sync` and `/v1/jobs/...`; media uses `/v1/media/{id}/{signature}`.
- Its sync operation is full-profile and retains only the latest receipt. This is not yet the common source-scoped durable-run model.
- Colony reuses portable Go connectors and synchronization primitives, while retaining provider-auth, PostgreSQL manifests/ownership and JobsAF.
- Colony's existing instance-scoped `provider-auths` and `import-jobs` APIs are not already the same management contract, and the companion PR does not already provide the common hosted media proxy.

**Do not describe the target architecture as already implemented.** Changes to the PRs must close the API, lifecycle, hosted proxy and client boundaries below.

Useful references at the reviewed Antfly revision:

- [Portable runner](https://github.com/antflydb/antfly/blob/c0ef17a66939ae4f6feb5a8eaa18417256bef769/go/pkg/sources/runner.go)
- [Text/media records](https://github.com/antflydb/antfly/blob/c0ef17a66939ae4f6feb5a8eaa18417256bef769/go/pkg/sources/document.go)
- [Shared synchronization protocol](https://github.com/antflydb/antfly/blob/c0ef17a66939ae4f6feb5a8eaa18417256bef769/go/pkg/sources/sync.go)
- [Current standalone service contract](https://github.com/antflydb/antfly/blob/c0ef17a66939ae4f6feb5a8eaa18417256bef769/specs/openapi/sources/api.yaml)
- [Generic native remote-content runtime](https://github.com/antflydb/antfly/blob/c0ef17a66939ae4f6feb5a8eaa18417256bef769/zig/pkg/antfly/src/common/remote_content_runtime.zig)
- [Existing connection vocabulary](https://github.com/antflydb/antfly/blob/c0ef17a66939ae4f6feb5a8eaa18417256bef769/zig/CONNECTIONS.md)

Related reliability/search context: [#1389](https://github.com/antflydb/antfly/issues/1389), [#1151](https://github.com/antflydb/antfly/issues/1151).

## Ownership boundaries

| Component | Owns |
| --- | --- |
| **Shared Go engine** | Provider connectors; metadata enumeration; original/explicit-export acquisition; revision/access validation; canonical text/media records; streaming verification; publication/visibility barriers; source ownership and authoritative deletion reconciliation. |
| **Standalone Go source CLI/server** | Operator authentication, local source/connection configuration, protected credential resolution, durable runs/checkpoints, locking/admission, cancellation/recovery and deployment of the media endpoint. |
| **Colony** | Tenant/instance/RBAC enforcement, provider-auth/OAuth and refresh lifecycle, PostgreSQL manifests/ownership, JobsAF execution/scheduling, quotas/billing, hosted publication and the media endpoint. |
| **Antfly** | Generic HTTP media retrieval and validation, extraction, chunking, embedding, indexing and queries. It does not need provider OAuth grants or provider-specific ingestion jobs. |
| **Source-management clients** | Common management operations against an explicit Go-server or Colony base URL with runtime-appropriate authentication. They do not enumerate providers or reconcile records. |

Colony calls shared Go libraries **in process**. It does not call a separately deployed standalone source server over HTTP, inherit the standalone keystore/operator-token model, or acquire a second scheduler.

Share the acquisition/reconciliation and media-delivery protocol, with adapters for credentials, receipts/authority, persistence and execution. Do not force Colony to use standalone filesystem state.

## Two API audiences

### Application-facing management API

One versioned OpenAPI contract defines shared source/run resources and operation semantics. A proposed mount is:

- Standalone: `https://source-service.example/sources/v1/...`
- Colony: `https://colony.example/api/v1/organizations/{org}/cloud/instances/{instance}/sources/v1/...`

These are **proposed paths**, not currently mounted routes. Finalize exact prefixes/versioning and compatibility before release.

Common operations should cover:

- Source creation, inspection, update and retirement, preserving stable ownership identity.
- Connection references and safe capability/health summaries.
- Source-scoped run submission, inspection, paginated durable history and cancellation.
- Resume of pinned selection versus restart/new selection.
- Explicit retain versus purge policy, durable deletion intent and progress.
- Structured safe errors, capability discovery and idempotent submission/recovery after a lost response.

A run's execution state is distinct from its publication outcome: a worker can finish with partial results. Only a fully verified authoritative inventory can authorize deletion. Expose this distinction explicitly.

Provider authorization remains runtime-specific: standalone protected secret installation/environment references versus Colony's existing OAuth/provider-auth workflow. The common API references authorized connections; it does not require a universal plaintext-secret endpoint. Colony-specific schedules, transforms and structured/unstructured import modes remain available as compatible extensions.

### Antfly-facing media-delivery protocol

Antfly fetches a published, version-bound representation from a Go or Colony media endpoint. This is a separate audience from the management API:

- A management token must not be embedded in a document/media URL.
- A media reference authorizes only its intended tenant/instance, source, object and selected representation/version.
- Possession of a connection ID alone grants no access.
- Provider credentials, refresh tokens and raw grants never enter document/catalog payloads.
- No endpoint accepts an arbitrary client URL and proxies it with ambient provider credentials.

Use one shared delivery protocol and Go implementation with runtime adapters. Standalone may continue signed capability URLs; define hosted capability issuance, verification and lifecycle with equivalent semantics. Finalize exact authentication/reference fields before release rather than assuming current signed URLs already solve all hosted isolation and lifecycle requirements.

## End-to-end flow

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    App[Application / source client] --> LocalAPI[Standalone management API]
    App --> CloudAPI[Colony management API]
    LocalAPI --> Local[Local durable runtime]
    CloudAPI --> Hosted[PostgreSQL / JobsAF runtime]
    Local --> Engine[Shared Go ingestion engine]
    Hosted --> Engine
    Engine --> Provider[Drive / S3 / GCS / other providers]
    Engine --> DB[Antfly records and catalog]
    DB --> Enrich[Antfly content processing]
    Enrich --> Media[Go or Colony media endpoint]
    Media --> Fetch[Shared Go provider fetch and verification]
    Fetch --> Provider
```

For a Drive folder:

1. The selected runtime creates/references a protected provider grant and stable ingestion connection.
2. It stores a source with folder selection, destination, publication policy and document permissions.
3. Its execution runtime runs the shared engine to enumerate metadata and acquire/verify selected content as needed.
4. The engine publishes explicit media rows referencing the runtime's media endpoint.
5. Antfly fetches those bytes over the media protocol; Go/Colony verifies current authority and selected representation before and during delivery.
6. Antfly processes the content. Its retry/repair paths retain the same representation identity.
7. Later authoritative runs reconcile changed/deleted objects only within the source's ownership.

Gmail, Slack and Discord acquisition also stays in Go. Binary attachments and explicitly supported immutable message/export representations can use the media protocol; ordinary normalized message text can remain text publication. Do not label generated message snapshots or Workspace exports as original binary files.

## Implementation work

### 1. Finalize the common schemas and compatibility strategy

- Define shared source, connection-reference, run, outcome/completeness, cancellation, purge, error and pagination schemas.
- Define idempotency-key scope, retention and payload matching. Lost acknowledgements must be resolved without launching duplicate work; clients do not blindly retry mutating operations.
- Define source update/configuration fencing, destination immutability and explicit migration behavior.
- Specify which operations are common and which are runtime extensions; advertise meaningful capabilities instead of silently changing behavior.
- Keep the source-management contract separate from the database OpenAPI.
- Preserve existing Go routes and Colony import clients through tested adapters, or document an intentional versioned migration.

### 2. Align standalone source-scoped execution and durable history

- Support per-source runs and durable receipts/history instead of silently syncing an entire profile and overwriting its only receipt.
- Keep complete profile/catalog context: selecting one source must not retire unrelated bindings or prune another source's media receipts.
- Preserve checkpoint/ownership state across restart, cancellation, credential rotation and source reconfiguration.
- Make run admission and idempotency durable, serialize overlapping writers, and fence an old run before a replacement can mutate or delete.
- Bound history queries, pagination, control responses and memory usage. Define retention explicitly.
- Preserve durable purge recovery, including provider-independent deletion and source-ID reuse rules.

Serialized standalone execution is an acceptable capability. A concurrent hosted scheduler is not required inside the local server.

### 3. Extract/reuse the shared media-delivery machinery

- Share object/representation identity, provider reads, access/version checks, strong content identity, conditional/range behavior and safe error mapping.
- Put runtime-specific credential resolution, current source/connection authority, receipt persistence and signing-key resolution behind explicit adapters.
- Keep source/run ownership in each runtime; the proxy must not independently invent a second source registry.
- Share provider clients safely with correct credential-generation invalidation, cancellation and bounded refresh/header/read deadlines.
- Preserve bounded buffering, backpressure, concurrency admission and cleanup on disconnect/failed verification.

Do not copy the entire standalone HTTP service or its filesystem/keystore into Colony.

### 4. Implement Colony's hosted management adapter and media endpoint

- Mount the common API under authenticated organization/instance scope and apply existing RBAC before resource access.
- Map existing source/import definitions and durable runs to the shared contract without losing schedules, transforms, structured/unstructured imports or legacy ownership migrations.
- Publish explicit hosted media references using the common delivery protocol.
- Resolve grants through provider-auth/OAuth, including refresh, rotation and revocation. Maintain clear authority rather than duplicate provider credentials in Antfly.
- Read current source/connection/publication authority from shared durable state; support multiple replicas and failover.
- Use shared signing-key lifecycle and receipt/authority state across replicas; do not rely on one node's disk or process-local keys.
- Enforce tenant/instance/source/object isolation and hosted resource/concurrency quotas.
- Connect dashboard configuration and source/run inspection to the same lifecycle.

Do not turn source catalog publication into an authorization database. Fetch authority comes from the runtime's protected state and policy.

### 5. Complete and test the media protocol

The published reference must distinguish:

- Canonical provider provenance/locator from the HTTP processing URL.
- Original binary bytes from a named export/derived representation.
- Selected provider revision/version from the content digest or delivery ETag.
- MIME, exact representation length and original/representation-byte SHA-256.

Required delivery behavior:

- Every read is bound to a valid source/object receipt and allowed connection/resource scope; recheck current authorization according to the documented policy.
- If the selected historical bytes cannot be retrieved, fail with a stable stale/unavailable result. Never substitute newer bytes under an old identity.
- Validate provider responses, ranges, exact lengths and final digest/revision before committing successful processing/cache state. A streaming consumer may receive provisional bytes; failed verification cannot be promoted as verified content.
- Define GET, HEAD, conditional and single-range behavior. HEAD must not accidentally report unverified replacement metadata; document when verification requires acquisition.
- Preserve identity through partial reads/ranges. A digest for an entire object is not the digest of a returned range.
- Define redirects explicitly; never forward secrets to an arbitrary redirect target.
- Define retryability and capacity/stale/revoked errors so Antfly can distinguish temporary unavailability from permanent invalidation.
- Treat capability URLs as sensitive; avoid logging full capability paths/query strings.
- Define authorization for source reconfiguration, removal, publication retirement, connection rotation/revocation and signing-key rotation. Keep the effect scoped to the intended source/connection.
- Support key rotation and old-reference retirement without silently breaking every unrelated published record.

**Proxy availability is a real dependency.** Later reads require the media runtime and provider to remain reachable and authorized. Restart/scale-out must preserve valid references, but this design cannot promise indefinite replay when provider history or access disappears. Do not mint short-lived URLs into durable records without an explicit refresh/republication mechanism. Define permanent failure, recovery/republication and capability retention rules.

Revocation stops future authorized reads according to the documented policy; it cannot recall bytes already delivered or automatically erase indexed content. Specify separately whether source removal retains rows/artifacts or queues their purge, and how provider permission changes trigger catalog/ACL maintenance. Do not imply provider revocation alone deletes prior indexed content.

### 6. Verify the generic Antfly consumption boundary

- Exercise existing HTTP source-reference fetching against both media implementations.
- Preserve representation identity, length, MIME, digest and conditional semantics through extraction, artifact scheduling, retries and repair.
- Bound fetch timeouts/resources and propagate safe stale/revoked/retryable failures instead of treating invalid content as success.
- Ensure proxy addresses are reachable from the workers and compatible with the existing outbound URL/redirect policy; avoid broadening arbitrary network access to make deployment work.
- Add only generic media-reference/HTTP-fetch changes that the integration proves are needed.

This work does **not** require native provider connectors, a native source-management API, native provider OAuth distribution, a database ingestion scheduler, or moving the Go engine to Zig.

### 7. Generate and package clients deliberately

- Generate shared Go models/interfaces and TypeScript/Python/Rust clients from the management spec.
- Put source management in a separate package or explicitly optional module/subpath, with an explicit management base URL and runtime-appropriate auth.
- The same common client operations target standalone or Colony; no automatic probing or accidental requests to the Antfly database listener.
- Keep runtime-specific connection authorization/configuration flows explicit.
- Preserve safe URL construction with instance prefixes, encoded identifiers, timeouts, redirect policy and structured errors.
- Applications use management operations. Antfly uses the media protocol; normal apps do not need to fetch raw capability URLs themselves.

## Correctness and performance invariants

- Only complete, authoritative, fully verified inventories authorize deletion; partial selections, failed reads, preflight rejection and ambiguous writes cannot.
- Source identity and owned key ranges remain stable; source-scoped runs and purge cannot affect sibling sources or application-owned rows.
- Existing visibility barriers, durable ownership journals, pinned selections, legacy migration and Colony attempt fences remain intact.
- A changed/unauthorized provider object never becomes the selected original merely because it is currently readable.
- Listing does not download bodies. Computing an original-byte SHA-256 requires a trusted checksum or verified acquisition; provider ETags are not automatically SHA-256.
- Reuse verified digest receipts only under the applicable version and authorization checks.
- No unsafe reliance on shared credential identity for document-sharing policy.
- Avoid unnecessary reacquisition for unchanged revisions; disclose any full-object verification required for HEAD/range requests.
- Bound active transfers, verification concurrency, buffering, durable control metadata, HTTP deadlines and provider-client caches. Enforce quotas across the intended hosted deployment, not just one replica.
- Cancellation, backpressure, blocked readers/writers and provider errors must release resources without accepting truncated content or losing recovery state.

## Reusable correctness and performance evidence

The following was validated for the reviewed PR revisions; it is evidence for those implementations, not qualification of the proposed shared management API or hosted media-delivery adapter.

- Full Antfly sources race suite and full Colony import race suite against isolated PostgreSQL 18 passed.
- Timeout and purge-recovery cases passed 20 repeated runs.
- Reviewed fixes verify Drive reader Close before staging upload, preserve exactly-once closure, and cancel aborted copies before cleanup.
- Purge completion persists the live filtered profile before clearing its tombstone, preventing source resurrection after an earlier profile-write failure and preserving concurrent credential revocation.
- Local exact-body merge preflight permits smaller siblings after budget rejection; failed/unverified items cannot authorize deletion or inventory promotion. Dispatched ambiguous writes still fence the writer.
- Original-byte verification streams with a 64 KiB buffer; the companion keeps at most a 1 MiB media window and four active fetches. S3/GCS retain one response per contiguous range; Drive uses revision-checked windows.
- The Google idle watchdog bounds headers/blocked reads while allowing progressing transfers and consumer backpressure. It reuses one timer; a synthetic 32 KiB read benchmark measured about 326 ns/read and 0 B/op, 0 allocations/op on an Apple M4 Max. This is not a network-throughput measurement.
- New immutable representations have a 30-minute verification deadline; companion gateway requests have a two-minute deadline; hosted staged-object operations have a ten-minute deadline. These are current bounds to preserve or deliberately redesign, not universal defaults for every future native deployment.
- The current branch's native server previously passed PDF publication → pinned fetch → extraction → chunking → full-text retrieval → revocation/purge integration, including preservation of unrelated application rows.
- Live cloud-provider credentials and model-backed embedding behavior were not qualified by those local tests. Full-service Colony integration was not green in the earlier attempt because required local services were absent and an unrelated migration test timed out; later ordinary Go packages and isolated PostgreSQL import tests passed.

Passing these tests does not qualify the shared management contract, Colony's media proxy, or their complete hosted lifecycle. Re-run the relevant checks against the final implementations.


## Delivery order and PR scope

1. **Agree on and land the shared management/media contracts**, adapter boundaries and compatibility tests.
2. **Antfly #1487:** align standalone per-source runs/history/idempotency, extract reusable proxy machinery, preserve media/listing/reconciliation behavior, and make source SDK packaging explicit.
3. **Colony #927:** consume that shared library/spec; implement tenant-scoped management adapters, hosted media authority/delivery, publication and credential lifecycle using existing PostgreSQL/JobsAF infrastructure.
4. **Integration:** prove both runtimes against Antfly's generic fetch/enrichment path and make any necessary generic consumer changes.
5. **Qualification/documentation:** run provider and lifecycle tests, document deployment/availability constraints and remove the original app workarounds.

Native provider connections/Drive fetching and mandatory durable staging are removed from the implementation plan. Optional future staging can implement the same immutable representation contract behind a different delivery adapter.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] One versioned management contract is implemented by both runtimes with explicit authentication, mounting and compatibility behavior.
- [ ] Common clients can configure/manage sources and inspect/start/cancel runs against either runtime using an explicit base URL.
- [ ] Runtime-specific provider authorization remains explicit; source records and media references contain no provider secrets.
- [ ] Standalone supports durable source-scoped execution/history, safe pagination and idempotent submission without retiring/pruning unrelated sources.
- [ ] Colony preserves organization/instance RBAC, OAuth/provider-auth, import modes/transforms, PostgreSQL ownership, JobsAF and existing scheduling.
- [ ] Both runtimes serve the same version-bound media protocol through shared Go code and runtime adapters.
- [ ] Hosted proxy references and authority survive restart/scale-out; cross-tenant/source/connection access is rejected.
- [ ] Media rows preserve provenance, selected representation/version, length, MIME and verified byte digest without fake extracted text.
- [ ] Antfly fetches and processes originals through the managed proxy without app-owned file routes or native Drive/email/chat connectors.
- [ ] Metadata-only docsaf listing downloads/exports no bodies.
- [ ] Stale versions, changed/truncated bytes, failed final verification and denied access cannot produce a successful verified processing result.
- [ ] Ranges/HEAD/conditional reads and redirects obey the documented version/authentication contract.
- [ ] Rotation/revocation/reconfiguration, capability/key lifecycle, retries and repair have tested semantics and preserve unrelated sources.
- [ ] Complete authoritative reconciliation deletes only owned records; partial/failed runs and lost acknowledgements cannot authorize unsafe cleanup.
- [ ] Retain/purge and crash recovery preserve ownership and cannot resurrect purged sources.
- [ ] Proxy/provider unavailability and loss of historical bytes produce visible recoverable/permanent outcomes according to the documented policy.
- [ ] Buffering/concurrency/deadlines/history are bounded; cancellation and stalled I/O release resources.
- [ ] SDK exports/docs correctly distinguish source-management endpoints from native database/inference APIs.
- [ ] Live provider and model-backed integration qualify the intended supported matrix; mocked/local tests are reported separately.
- [ ] No native ingestion control plane, provider-specific Antfly connector or mandatory staging service is required.

## Decisions to settle in the contracts

- Exact management and media route mounts, versioning and legacy-route migration.
- Shared source configuration versus hosted extensions; canonical outcome/completeness and purge semantics.
- Idempotency retention/scope, source configuration fencing and run-history retention/pagination.
- Media reference/authentication fields, capability lifetime, key rotation and replica-safe receipt storage.
- Provider-specific revision/export guarantees and behavior when historical content is unavailable.
- Whether runtime permissions are checked per request or through a bounded maintained authority lease, with explicit revocation guarantees.
- Retry/repair/republication policy for stale or retired references.
- Separate package versus optional SDK module/subpath.

items.body:
**Spec:** §14 Epic 6, ticket 6.2 · implements §3.1, §7.9, §5.3 · extended by ADR-0006, ADR-0008
**Size:** 2–8 h
**Layer:** `Whetstone.Worker` — jobs dispatched through the outbox. The web app initiates the soft delete; it never issues the purge.
**Blocked by:** #34 (2.11 Outbox dispatcher), #102 (OQ-9 — corpus ingestion mode), #89 (6.4 audit log)

## Changed by the strategy shift

The system now stores **private source code**. The purge surface grew accordingly, and one new rule
comes with it: **content goes, provenance stays.**

> ADR-0006, Consequences → Bad — "Corpus ingestion is a new trust boundary — the system now reads
> private source code. Every §7 control applies to the corpus, and **`BeforeState` is as sensitive
> as `reviews.answer_text`** for retention purposes."

> ADR-0008, Consequences → Bad — "Storage grows monotonically — retired exercises are kept forever.
> Bounded by GDPR retention (spec §7.9), which **purges `BeforeState` content** … **leaving the
> provenance record.**"

Provenance carries no content — `SourceKind`, `SourceRef`, `ContentHash`, `GeneratedAt` — and it is
what keeps a retired exercise's review history resolvable. Purging it destroys the audit trail
ADR-0008 was written to protect. Purging the content is the obligation.

## Goal
GDPR erasure, self-service, with a real purge: after 30 days the rows are gone — from the corpus
surface as much as from `reviews`.

## Shape

`Whetstone.Worker`

```
PurgeDeletedUserJob     RunAsync(TenantId, UserId, CancellationToken) : Task<PurgeResult>
PurgeDeletedTenantJob   RunAsync(TenantId, CancellationToken)         : Task<PurgeResult>
```

Legal transitions, and there are no others:

```
Active  →  SoftDeleted            immediate, user-initiated, reversible
SoftDeleted  →  Active            within 30 days only (UX-10)
SoftDeleted  →  Purged            after 30 days, by the job
Purged  →  ✗                      terminal. Nothing returns from here
```

**The surface to purge.** Personal data, as before: cards, reviews (`answer_text`,
`rubric_result`), sessions, `mastery_snapshots`, `ai_usage`, identity rows, and audit events where
the subject is the user. Plus, new:

| Holds | Purge | Keep |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `exercise_candidates` | `before_state`, `finding`, `rationale` | the row, its state, its `provenance` |
| Corpus content at rest | everything — whatever form OQ-9 settles on | — |
| Corpus access credentials | the token, at tenant deletion | — |
| Exercises derived from the tenant's corpus | prompt, rubric, reference answer | the row, its state, its `provenance` |
| `provenance` | — | all of it |

**`PurgeResult`** reports per-table counts. The test asserts against it, and it is what makes
"purge means rows gone" checkable rather than asserted.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] **Self-service account deletion**, **soft-delete immediately**, **hard purge after 30 days** via `PurgeDeletedUser` / `PurgeDeletedTenant` (§5.3)
- [ ] **Purge means rows gone** — including from **`mastery_snapshots`** and **`ai_usage`**. Append-only is an application rule (§4.4), not an exemption from erasure
- [ ] **New:** purge removes **corpus content at rest** for a deleted tenant, in whatever form OQ-9 lands on — a clone, an index, cached blobs, or all three
- [ ] **New:** purge removes **`exercise_candidates.before_state`, `.finding`, and `.rationale`** — these are as sensitive as `answer_text` and are literally the customer's source code
- [ ] **New:** purge revokes and removes the tenant's **corpus access credential**. A deleted tenant whose token still works is an ongoing unauthorised access, not a data-retention issue
- [ ] **Provenance rows survive the purge**, and so do exercise and candidate rows stripped of content. State this in the deletion confirmation — the user is told what remains and why
- [ ] **Purge verified by a test** asserting zero remaining rows, or zero remaining content columns, across **every** table holding personal data or corpus content
- [ ] The table list is **one list**, shared with the export (#86) and the retention job (#88), so the three cannot drift apart
- [ ] The job is **idempotent** (§5.3) and safe under duplicate outbox delivery
- [ ] A purge writes an `audit_event` recording what was purged and how many rows (#89) — the audit event is the surviving evidence that erasure happened
- [ ] **UX-10:** the destructive action is confirmed and **reversible for 30 days** — which is exactly what the soft-delete window provides, and the confirmation says so with the date

## Tests — properties, not procedures
- [ ] `Purge_leaves_no_row_in_any_table_holding_personal_data`
- [ ] `Purge_leaves_no_corpus_content_anywhere_at_rest`
- [ ] `Purge_clears_before_state_finding_and_rationale_on_every_candidate_of_the_tenant`
- [ ] `Purge_retains_every_provenance_row`
- [ ] `Purge_revokes_the_tenant_corpus_credential`
- [ ] `Purge_is_idempotent_under_duplicate_delivery`
- [ ] `A_soft_deleted_user_is_restorable_within_thirty_days`
- [ ] `A_purged_user_cannot_be_restored`
- [ ] `The_purge_table_list_and_the_export_table_list_are_the_same_list`

## Context

**Failure modes worth knowing before you start:**
- **The table you forgot.** This is the entire risk. A purge that misses one table is a breach you find out about from somebody else, months later, and there is no partial credit. The test asserting against a shared, enumerated list is the only defence that survives future schema changes.
- **Cascade versus explicit.** Relying on `ON DELETE CASCADE` means the purge's correctness lives in a migration nobody reads. Whichever you choose, the test must not be able to pass because of a cascade you did not know about.
- **The purge racing a live job.** `SnapshotMastery` (#80) writing a row for a user mid-purge resurrects deleted personal data. So does an in-flight grading handler (#62), and so does a drift run regenerating a candidate.
- **RLS and the purge role.** The job runs across a tenant that is being destroyed. It needs privileges the request path does not have. Getting that wrong in the permissive direction is a tenancy hole (#28, #29); getting it wrong in the restrictive direction is a purge that silently does nothing and reports success.
- **Backups.** A restored backup (#93) contains the purged rows. The retention of backups is a documented, bounded window, or the purge is theatre.
- **Blocked on OQ-9.** You cannot enumerate corpus data at rest until the ingestion mode is decided (#102). Clone-and-index leaves a lot on disk; read-only API per query leaves much less. The purge is different work in each case.

## Working agreement (§17)

Hand-built, `security`. This is deletion correctness — on the §17 list as both "anything
security-critical" and "tenancy". It is also the only ticket in Epic 6 whose failure mode is a
regulatory one.

The exercise is enumerating a surface completely under adversarial self-questioning — *"what else
holds this user's data?"* — and then building a test that keeps the answer true after the schema
moves. That is a judgement skill, it is asked about in interviews, and an agent that generates a
list from the current schema produces something that is correct today and quietly wrong at the next
migration.

If you break the rule, log it in `docs/ai-log.md`.

items.title: [Research][Decision Models] Reciprocal Agent Memory value for Jev/TypeSafe, Rune and other providers
items.body:
## Purpose

Qualify whether **Agent Memory is valuable as a persistent governed context and decision-history layer to specialized decision-model developers and the applications built on their models**, beginning with TypeSafe AI's Jev. This is the **reciprocal direction** not fully owned by #644 (Jev-Mem mechanism harvest) or #495 (model-for-Agent-Memory benchmarks). Compare vendors on actual need and technical evidence, not on Decision Index placement or presumed willingness to partner.

**No outreach, commercial commitment, paid usage, model acquisition, production runtime dependency, or default-on integration is authorized by this issue.** Keep evaluation in local/reproducible and approved environments; no unapproved GitHub Actions.

## Existing work, not to duplicate

- #644 — Jev-Mem source/architecture harvest, provider-neutral System-One controller and shadow retrieval. Jev-Mem is an independent memory-research implementation ancestry; it **does not prove TypeSafe AI provides or endorses that memory product**.
- #490 — completed provider-neutral classification boundary.
- #495 — open live provider/model comparison on Agent Memory-native classification tasks.
- #601 — open same-harness *memory-system* comparator league (not decision-model vendor partnerships).
- #780 — Fastino GLiDE and GLiNER reciprocal investigation; reuse common harness, evaluation rules, context budget constraints, and decision outcome definitions rather than duplicating.
- #153 — precedent-memory semantics (historical approvals are evidence, never standing authorization).
- Existing controller contract: `reference/fixtures/runtime/system-one-controller-contract-v1.json`. Hosted decision models may only estimate/propose; host owns scope, admission, lifecycle, PAMA and history.

## Candidate register (evidence + initial disposition)

1. **TypeSafe AI / Jev** — **P1, detailed reciprocal qualification.** Official product: https://typesafe.ai ; Jev is a hosted System-One model consuming caller-supplied state/questions and returning typed decisions with probabilities. Direct opportunity: persistent contextual state, historical outcomes, corrected/current facts and governed decision precedents for Jev-powered apps. Do not confuse an independent API gateway with TypeSafe's official API or the independent Jev-Mem repository. Verify current native memory features, developer/platform strategy, pricing/data-handling terms, and target applications before suggesting any partner proposition.
2. **Invergent / Surogate Rune v3** — **P2, technical + reciprocal research**: https://huggingface.co/michaelfeil/rune-26b-a4b ; https://github.com/invergent-ai/surogate . Public Apache-2.0 labeled weights (verify original upstream licenses and conditions, exact revision and runtime requirements), typed choice/noul/score, long-context multimodal decision context. Opportunity: local/offline decision engine augmented by governed memory, compare long-context-only vs retriever/RAG vs Agent Memory. Unlike tiny local classifiers, a 26B model has substantial hosting cost; don't assume it fits small consumer GPUs.
3. **Decider chat / Mapika** — **P3 conditional**: https://huggingface.co/Mapika/decider-chat-gemma4-31b . Described as a decision readout of Gemma-4 31B with unchanged underlying weights and fitted calibration. Assess if implementation/author represents a practical integration/collaboration entity; larger model hosting could outweigh value.
4. **AutoJev, Jebadiah, Eikos, simple-jev, and newly ranked models** — **discovery queue only**. Authenticate upstream owner, revisions, license, actual model availability, permissible inference, and real integration surface. No partner proposition without a real organization/developer and usable code/API.
5. **Fastino GLiDE** — stays under #780; reference results in the shared comparative matrix, not a second Fastino issue.

## Two-way research questions

A. **Model -> Agent Memory** (owned primarily by #495 and #644): does a specialized decision model improve typed memory admission proposals, relation estimation, retrieval routing, evidence sufficiency, contradiction detection, or consolidation proposals while respecting memory authority and cost?

B. **Agent Memory -> model developer / model user** (this issue): does governed persistent memory improve *decision outcomes* in cross-session, state-changing or policy-sensitive applications of an otherwise stateless decision API, compared with recent-context, rolling history, simple RAG, or the vendor's native memory? Does storing evidence provenance, correction/supersession, invalidity, deletion, and decision outcomes create unique value rather than retrievable clutter?

C. **Product/partnership feasibility**: is there demonstrable customer value for a reference architecture, optional SDK adapter, marketplace/service listing, community demo, or commercial integration? Where does the vendor already compete? Would the integration need to be API-level, on-prem/offline, or sidecar? Do not assume mutual interest.

## Sequential acceptance plan

### 1. Dated vendor/product inventory
- [ ] Pin first-party TypeSafe Jev product/API docs and verify Jev memory support (presence, absence, or UNKNOWN).
- [ ] Pin Rune/Surogate/Decider upstream sources, rights, runtimes, context & question limits, price/local feasibility.
- [ ] Distinguish model product, third-party memory research, gateway reseller, and public community demonstration.
- [ ] Build verified/uncertain/unsupported matrix: technical capability, owner, license, tenancy/privacy, security, available provider, prospective user need, distinctiveness, expected effort.
- [ ] Rank additional candidates by *use-case fit and feasibility*, not benchmark rank.

### 2. Provider-neutral bidirectional experiment
- [ ] Reuse #780's mock multi-session, changing-policy decision workload and preregistered fixture/gold; ensure decision models get identical tasks, options, permissible context budget, and outcome evaluator.
- [ ] Same-provider four context ablations: recent only, naive rolling summary/history, simple RAG, Agent Memory governed package. Repeat for Jev, GLiDE (through #780), and Rune/other feasible model. No unreproducible cross-provider comparisons.
- [ ] Cross provider and context axis (factorial) to separate model effect, memory effect, and interaction. Reject vendor-specific prompt hacks.
- [ ] Measure error/regret, policy violations, stale fact and disallowed-data reliance, correct abstention, persistence/corrections, evidence relevance, latency p50/p95, context size, full ingestion+retrieval+decision cost and failed-response rate.
- [ ] Evaluate "memory not needed" zero/short-history controls to avoid overstating utility.
- [ ] Review privacy/retention/API data-egress constraints; use synthetic or authorized public datasets only.
- [ ] Fail-closed malformed/controller responses, scoped admission and deletion, and typed provenance remain non-negotiable. No vendor model gives itself memory authority.
- [ ] Distinguish shadow adapter correctness from actual enforced runtime improvement. Agent Memory has a qualified bounded single-host SQLite profile, not general production/enterprise scale.

### 3. Partner-fit and outputs
- [ ] Produce TypeSafe/Jev-specific 1-page opportunity map: hypothesized product problem; whether already solved; concrete minimal joint demo; differential evidence; integration friction; product maturity; independent implementation viability.
- [ ] Qualify Rune and other viable vendors with same scorecard; separate strong *technical* fit from plausible *partner* fit.
- [ ] Reconcile common evaluation evidence to #495, #780 and the canonical dashboard; never score decision benchmark and memory benchmark in a single aggregate.
- [ ] Recommend pursue/defer/reject by vendor and state what would be needed for outreach. Do not contact vendors without owner approval.

## Completion

An auditable model-provider candidate matrix, a Jev reciprocal-value brief, a reusable frozen cross-session decision benchmark design and runnable/blocked evidence as applicable, and a prioritized disposition for other candidates. Real partnership opportunity requires a reproducible, meaningful *incremental end-to-end improvement* over reasonable alternatives, not merely a leaderboard score.

**Status at creation (2026-10-13):** provider/repo discovery only; no new live model inference, bidirectional benchmarks, partnership contact, or production integration completed.
