items.title: Tracking: move multitenancy from sharded (one process per collection, per-tenant tables and shard keys) to non-sharded (shared structures served by any process)

labels.name: refactor
labels.description: Code refactoring that doesn't add new features.

labels.name: keep-open
labels.description: Prevents the auto-close task from closing this issue.

labels.name: horizontal scaling
labels.description: Wrong or unsafe when more than one server process serves the same backends (replicas or workers)

items.body:
### Where to start (status 2026-10-02)

**Storage layer.** Segment store: done (#1661 on main). Qdrant and Milvus: #1733 -> #1734 -> #1735 -> #1736 in review (SQL collection registry, an incarnation per collection life, fenced handles, claimed purge); they close #1524, #1525 and #1563 on merge. SQLite stores: #1536 stays with the SQLite store fixes (#1460 to #1675), and they are HOST or PROCESS scope by declaration (#1757).

**Above the stores**, in priority order. Each is a tracking issue with a one-glance table (what is wrong, best fix, order) and a PR split, and each child issue shows its tracker at the top.

1. #1755 Session lifecycle: the `sessions` row as registry plus durable jobs. Tracks #1543, #1571, #1575, #1576, #1577, #1600, #1655, #1728, #1749.
2. #1756 Background work: one claimable-job primitive for provision, delete, ingestion and purge. Tracks #1745, #1749, #1699, #1738, #1722.
3. #1757 Concurrency scope per component, so declarative memory and short-term memory stay available for single-replica deployments without a routing layer. Tracks #1748, #1753, #1745.
3. #1758 Replica-safe defaults in one change. Tracks #1746, #1747, #1730, #1750, #1751, #1752, #1754.

Design reference: #1579 (deferred as a whole; its vocabulary and target shapes are what the tracking issues cite).

**Labels.** `horizontal scaling`: wrong or unsafe with more than one server process on the same backends. `concurrency`: wrong under concurrent requests or processes regardless of replica count (races, lost updates, unarbitrated read-then-write). `recovery`: a failure or crash leaves durable state nothing repairs (partial writes, lost jobs, no retry or terminal state). An issue carries every label that applies.

### Why this issue exists

The issues linked below were filed one at a time, most of them as bugs. Read individually they look like an accumulation of unrelated defects in the storage layer. Read together they are one change of model: the codebase was built for **sharded** horizontal scaling (each logical collection or partition owned by exactly one process, and separated from other tenants by a physical structure of its own), and the requirement is now **non-sharded** scaling (any process serves any tenant, and tenants are rows or values inside structures they share). This issue states that change once, records why the previous model was there, classifies each linked issue against it, and tracks what remains.

### The model the codebase was built on, and why

Two decisions, both explicit and documented when they were made.

**1. Ownership by process sharding.** #1201 (merged 2026-04-02) set the `VectorStore` contract that is still in `common/vector_store/vector_store.py` today:

> A given logical collection identified by a (namespace, name) pair must be managed by at most one process at a time. The consumer is responsible for sharding names across processes.

Its description states the guarantees plainly: "safe concurrent usage on a single process" and "safe concurrent sharded usage (one node per logical collection) on multiple processes". With ownership fixed per process, lifecycle operations (create, open-or-create, delete) could be read-check-write sequences guarded by per-process `asyncio` locks, and backends without transactions or unique constraints (Qdrant, Milvus) could keep their catalog of logical collections inside the backend itself. The multi-process guarantee was correct under its contract and was never broken: strict sharding always worked. The restriction itself is what became the limitation (#1524, #1525).

**2. Per-tenant physical structures.** #1205 (merged 2026-05-08) scoped the event memory "by partition key: should allow sharding and horizontal scaling", and on PostgreSQL gave every segment-store partition its own pair of child tables under LIST-partitioned parents, created and dropped by per-tenant DDL. #1292 (merged 2026-05-02) gave every SQLite vector collection its own tables, for a stated reason: "Partition keys are avoided in favor of per-collection tables, since sqlite-vec ANN indexes may not support them." Qdrant's `is_distributed` flag gives every logical collection its own shard key. The payoff was real: deleting a tenant was one `DROP` rather than a row-scanning `DELETE`, one tenant's rows never interleaved with another's in a heap or index, and backend index limitations were sidestepped. Note that #1201 already rejected one native collection per tenant ("most vector databases recommend against one collection per tenant, and empirical tests show that many collections induces significant overhead"); the per-tenant structure was the shard key or child table beneath a shared native collection, not the collection itself.

Both decisions fit the deployments they served: a single server process, embedded SQLite as a first-class backend, an opt-in pre-GA event backend, and tenant counts at which per-tenant DDL was cheap. Nothing below should be read as those decisions having been mistakes at the time.

### What changed

Two requirements the sharded model does not meet:

- **Multiple server processes must serve the same tenants.** Any replica handles any session; routing by session affinity is not a requirement a hosted deployment can carry. This is the horizontal-scalability problem as restated in #1524 and #1525: multiple processes working the *same* collections and partitions, not more processes each owning their own.
- **Tenant counts of tens of thousands to millions**, with individual tenants ranging from tens of thousands to tens of millions of rows (`design/segment_store_shared_tables.md` in #1545).

### Why the sharded model fails them

Measured, in the linked issues and in the design doc:

| Cost of the model | Evidence |
| --- | --- |
| Per-tenant DDL on shared PostgreSQL parents | #1544's second half, and the design doc in #1545: create and delete DDL deadlocked with writers and with each other, on upstream and on every intermediate fix, in two cycle shapes; the class has nowhere to live once there is no lifecycle DDL. (#1544's first half, a `CASCADE` that removed the shared foreign key, is a plain bug; see the classification below.) |
| Per-tenant partitions and prepared statements | #1546: after five executions PostgreSQL switches to a generic plan that locks every child partition per read: 9 locks per read with a custom plan, 319 with the generic plan at 316 partitions, HTTP 500 `out of shared memory` at 128-way concurrency. Each per-tenant table also costs about 5 catalog relations and disk files, which does not survive the required tenant counts. |
| Per-tenant shard keys on Qdrant | #1564: 450 ms per tenant admission, 45 s for 100 tenants against 0.3 s with payload partitioning, 505 segments against 5, and cluster mode required. |
| Per-process ownership | #1524, #1525: the moment two processes manage the same name, lock-guarded read-check-write lifecycle has no arbiter. #1566 (folded into #1564): the in-process lock table was a leftover of that serialisation. |

The comparison that settled the segment store (raw asyncpg, 40 tenants x 2000 row-pairs, pgvector:pg16, 2 CPUs; full table in the design doc):

| layout | ingest | seed read | tenant create | catalog cost |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `PARTITION OF` children | 8.7-9.2k pairs/s | 0.43-0.46 ms | ~12 ms DDL | ~5 relations/tenant |
| shared tables | 15k pairs/s | 0.21 ms | 0.006 ms | none |

Per-tenant tables won only small-tenant removal latency (9 ms drop against 58 ms row delete), which does not justify their catalog cost at the required tenant counts. This is the industry's pool model: O(1) logical deletion via a registry plus asynchronous batched reclamation; O(1) physical drops exist only in per-tenant-resource (silo) architectures, which the tenant-count requirement excludes.

### The target model

The layer above the stores that ties these together (a tenant record with a step table and a reconciler, UUID-only store keys minted per tenant lifetime, a single tenant handle, and prompt purge as best-effort) is proposed in `design/tenant_lifecycle.md` under #1579, with the resource-level contracts the stores expose to it. The bullets below are the store-level targets that proposal builds on.

- **A tenant is a row, not a relation.** One registry row per live tenant, carrying a random `incarnation` minted at creation; data rows and records are keyed by the incarnation. Creating a tenant is an insert.
- **One physical structure per backend, shared by every tenant**: shared tables on SQL; payload-partitioned native collections on vector backends, with native collections shared by config as #1201 already did.
- **Lifecycle arbitrated by the database, so any process may perform it**: unique constraints decide create races, row locks serialise delete against in-flight writers, `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` lets concurrent purgers split a backlog.
- **Deletion is O(1) logical** (registry delete plus a purge-queue entry in one transaction); **physical reclamation is asynchronous**, bounded per call, safe to run from any process, and driven by a background purger.
- **Stale handles cannot reach a successor.** A handle carries the incarnation it was opened on. Where the backend can pin a registry row (the segment store, with `FOR SHARE`), a stale handle raises; where it cannot (the vector backends), a stale handle's writes land in a dead incarnation that nothing reads and reclamation removes, with lease validation against the registry as the remaining option (#1563, #1564). Either way a tenant recreated under the same key is unreachable from the old handle, on any process, without coordination.
- **The contract says what each store supports.** The blanket "at most one process" sentence goes; a store whose metadata moves to a cross-process authority says so, and a deployment can introspect what it may do instead of relying on out-of-band knowledge (#1524, #1525).
- **Native containers are provisioned, not created on the request path.** Creating a logical collection is one registry insert arbitrated by a primary key; the container it lands in already exists, shaped once per deployment (one schema per container, because a shared container cannot carry per-tenant schemas) and ensured by the same provisioning step that owns SQL schema (#1572, #1573, #1570).
- **Per-tenant physical isolation stays available as a tier** for an oversized tenant (Qdrant's tiered multitenancy, per #1564), never as the default.

### Status by component

Each row names the issues that carry the work; fixes and their state are tracked on those issues, not here.

| Component | Sharded model | Target | Issues |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Segment store, PostgreSQL | LIST-partitioned parents, per-tenant child tables and DDL | shared tables keyed by incarnation; registry and purge queue; writers pin the registry row | #1544, #1546, #1549 |
| Segment store, SQLite | shared tables keyed by partition key (never sharded), no fencing | same architecture on every dialect | #1549 |
| Vector store lifecycle, all backends | per-backend ad-hoc catalogs, per-process locks; contract forbids multi-process management | collection metadata arbitrated by a cross-process authority, so any process can create, open and delete; the contract states what each store supports | #1524, #1525 |
| Vector store create path and interface | native container created inside `create_collection` (a dual write across registry and backend, safe only because names are content-addressed); per-collection `VectorStoreCollectionConfig` promising per-tenant schemas | containers provisioned before serving; `create_collection` is a registry insert; collection shape configured per deployment | #1572, #1573 |
| Qdrant | `is_distributed` shard key per logical collection; native name re-derived from `sha256(config)` on every open; in-process lock table | payload partitioning; native name pinned at creation; lifecycle arbitrated by the cross-process authority; reclamation of dead partition keys | #1564, #1565, #1563, #1562 (#1566 folded into #1564) |
| SQLite vector stores | per-collection tables; stale handles reach the successor | incarnation-scoped native resources (per-collection tables stay; the store's stated reason is that sqlite-vec's index may not support a partition key) | #1536 |
| Milvus | per-record `partition_key` field filtered on queries (already value-based); catalog in a dummy-vector `__registry` collection | catalog moved to the cross-process authority | #1524, #1535 |
| Session data manager | read-then-write on session rows, safe only with one process per session | database-arbitrated create and update | #1543 |
| Schema provisioning | every process runs `create_all` at boot; no migration path for a layout change | one provisioning owner; migrations carry layout changes such as the segment store's | #1570 |
| Above the stores | process-local handle caches; no domain-error-to-status mapping | evict and re-resolve on a stale handle; explicit API status | #1571 |

Found along the way, not sharding-related, but blocking correctness on SQLite: #1568 (per-connection state registered per store on caller-supplied engines) and #1542 (engines built without WAL, busy timeout, or explicit write transactions). Contract issues that matter more once native collections are shared across tenants: #1534 (unbounded property-key cardinality, undeclared-property mandate) and #1535 (`indexed_properties_schema` is part of collection identity); #1573 narrows that to whether per-collection configuration belongs in the interface at all.

### How to read the linked issues

- **Plain defects, unrelated to the model**: #1544's first half (a `CASCADE` that removes a shared constraint), #1562 (config serialisation repoints data), #1568 (per-connection SQLite state registered late).
- **Handle bugs the sharded model could have fixed locally**: #1536, #1549, #1563. Each reproduces inside one process: an in-flight request holds a handle while that same process deletes and recreates the collection, and the handle reaches the successor. Real under any model, but not a failure of sharding: the owning process performs the delete and could invalidate every handle it issued at that moment, in memory. The target model removes that option, since the deleter may be another process, so invalidation moves into the data as the incarnation.
- **Costs of the sharded model that only surface at scale**: #1546, #1564, #1544's second half (lifecycle DDL deadlocking against shared parents), #1566 (in-process lifecycle serialisation), and the catalog cost per tenant. Not coding errors; the model's own behaviour under tenant counts and process counts it was not designed for.
- **Capability gaps the sharded model never had to fill**: #1524, #1525 (cross-process lifecycle arbitration), #1565 (reclamation, since a value cannot be dropped), #1543 (lost updates once two processes share a session), #1570 (a schema owner, once tenant metadata is rows and only the fixed boot-time schema is left), #1572 (a provisioning owner for native containers, once creating a collection is a registry insert).
- **Consequences of the target model**: #1571 (fencing makes staleness recognisable, so the layers above must handle it), #1573 (a shared container carries one schema, so the interface must stop promising one per collection), the asynchronous-erasure semantics (a deleted tenant is unreachable immediately and erased in the background, so synchronous erasure is a deployment's explicit choice).

### Done when

- The "at most one process" clause is gone from `vector_store.py`, replaced by a scope every store declares and honours.
- No backend creates a per-tenant physical structure by default; tenant creation is a row write everywhere, and the per-tenant tier is an explicit opt-in.
- Every lifecycle operation is safe from any process on the same backend: create races resolve by constraint, delete is idempotent and fences in-flight writers, purge is concurrent-safe and bounded.
- A stale handle cannot reach a successor tenant on any backend (raising where the backend can pin a registry row, landing in a dead incarnation where it cannot), and every backend has reclamation for dead tenants.
- Native containers are provisioned before serving and creating a logical collection is a single registry insert; collection shape is configured per deployment, one schema per container.
- Existing deployments have a stated path for each layout change: a migration through #1570's infrastructure, or an explicit recreate-schema statement of the kind the segment store overhaul makes for the pre-GA event backend.

### Out of scope

- The declarative (Neo4j and Nebula) backend: audited 2026-10-02 (#1753); kept for single-replica deployments by scope declaration (#1757), not made to scale.
- Cross-replica coherence of the process-local `EpisodicMemoryManager` cache: moved into #1755 (step 5, instances hold no per-session state once short-term memory is process-scoped, #1757). #1297, which rated it the main scaling bottleneck, is closed.

*Investigated and written by Claude (Claude Code), filed from the account of the user who commissioned the investigation.*

items.body:
## Outcome

Deliver an optional, self-hosted internal fleet dashboard for SysWarden v5.00.0. Give operators a coherent fleet inventory, supported L2-L7 alerts, approved administration, rate-based KPIs, controlled exports and an interactive 2D world map for the External fleet. Separate External and Internal fleet navigation using explicit exposure and hosting metadata. Match the official SysWarden visual identity across every screen.

Parent roadmap: #222. Owner-approved scope addition recorded on October 12, 2026. This is work package 18, planned for milestone `v5.00.0`. It is not an implemented feature, a security certification or a measured capacity claim. Coordinate planning with the October 15 v5 resumption.

The console runs in an enterprise management network. Local SysWarden protection and CLI/TUI operation remain independent of its availability. Internal network placement does not establish trust. This scoped addition supersedes the previous blanket browser-administration exclusion in #222 and #223; it does not authorize an Internet-facing console or unrestricted fleet orchestration.

## Preferred architecture and trust boundaries

Record the final choices in a reviewed ADR before implementation. The preferred starting design is:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    B[Authorized browser] -->|HTTPS, same-origin session| C[Unprivileged Go console]
    C -->|OIDC code flow with PKCE| I[Enterprise identity provider]
    N[Explicitly enrolled nodes] -->|Outbound mTLS, bounded observations| R[Authenticated read-plane ingestion]
    R --> P[Bounded fleet projection]
    C -->|Scope-checked reads| P
    C -->|Exact plan and human approval| A[Separate response authorization boundary]
    A -->|Expiring typed transactions over authenticated channel| N
    N -->|Verified outcomes| R
    A --> E[Durable audit and signed evidence]
```

- **Optional central component:** a separately packaged Go service using escaped templates and embedded, versioned assets. Use progressive enhancement with small browser modules. No Node.js runtime, external CDN, remote fonts, analytics, Kubernetes, Redis or Elasticsearch requirement. Do not start a web server on every protected node or revive a browser terminal/ttyd interface.
- **One fleet trust contract:** reuse and extend #233 enrollment, mutual authentication, node/cluster/epoch identity, replay protection, rotation and revocation. Prefer node-initiated outbound connections so managed nodes need no new inbound administration listener. Explicit enrollment and endpoint allowlists prevent implicit discovery and arbitrary-target proxying or SSRF.
- **Same-origin browser boundary:** browser sessions never receive agent credentials or connect directly to protected nodes. Use normal authenticated requests for actions and a bounded, multiplexed server-sent event channel for updates. Cursors carry position, not authority; authorize initial subscription, replay, reconnect and subsequent scope changes, with prompt revocation.
- **Small persistent footprint:** start with a single active console and local SQLite WAL for bounded projections and durable job metadata, with journal/evidence contracts from #225 and #232. Bound queues, queries, retention, replay and export work. Never share a WAL database across machines or use a network filesystem. Freeze the final storage choice after the capacity benchmark. Active-active operation requires a separate reviewed storage and fencing design.
- **Safe recovery:** document consistent backup, restore, projection rebuild and certificate recovery. Restoring a backup must fence stale epochs and invalidate pending approvals or jobs that could replay privileged work. Protect audit retention; disk pressure must be visible and must prevent unsafe new mutations rather than silently discard mandatory evidence.
- **Independent protection:** console, database, network or identity-provider outages must not disable local enforcement. Deny new privileged console actions when authority cannot be established. Existing bounded controls follow their locally enforced expiry and recovery contract.

## Authentication, authorization and host hardening

- Use a maintained OIDC implementation with authorization-code flow, PKCE S256, exact redirect validation and issuer/audience/state/nonce checks. Require enterprise MFA for privileged roles and reviewed step-up authentication for sensitive actions. Do not implement a custom identity protocol or ship default administrator credentials.
- Keep identity-provider tokens server-side. Use secure, HttpOnly session cookies with a reviewed SameSite policy, bounded idle and absolute lifetimes, logout and revocation. No bearer tokens in browser local storage or query strings. Protect CSRF, cross-origin requests, framing and content injection; deploy a restrictive CSP without arbitrary inline scripts.
- Deny access by default. Use exactly four dashboard roles: Administrator (`admin`), Supervisor (`supervisor`), Read-only (`read-only`) and Approver (`approver`), scoped to explicit node groups. Enforce permissions server-side for every object, aggregate, map marker, stream, cursor, export and download. A hidden button is not authorization. Apply scope before computing any aggregate so charts cannot disclose unauthorized nodes.
- Separate enrollment, identity administration, observation and response authority. A read-plane identity, a compromised node or a read-only browser session must not authorize fleet changes. Critical actions require independent approval by a different authorized principal under enterprise policy; the initiator cannot approve its own critical request.
- Run the console without root or a fleet SSH key, with minimal filesystem access, service sandboxing and SELinux compatibility. Use verified TLS, an explicit management bind address, bounded requests and timeouts, and explicit trusted-proxy configuration. Do not open host firewall ports automatically. Do not disable certificate validation or host hardening to make deployment work.
- Treat node names, labels, alert fields and geographic metadata as untrusted input. Escape text and validate schema, lengths, coordinates and addresses. Audit enrollment, role changes, sensitive reads/exports, approvals and verified outcomes without logging secrets or raw sensitive payloads.

### Four-role permission matrix

Owner decision recorded on October 21, 2026: the dashboard has exactly four roles. The English UI names and stable identifiers below implement Admin, Superviseur, Read-only and Approbateur. There is no separate viewer, analyst or operator role. Node-group scope and operation-specific policy refine these four roles; they do not introduce extra roles or grant global fleet authority.

| Role | Permitted workflow within authorized scope | Explicit limits |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Administrator (`admin`) | Manage approved accounts/scopes and enrollment; read, draft and validate configuration; execute approved typed changes and supported recovery/rollback. | Cannot bypass validation, ownership, MFA or approval; cannot approve its own critical request, including through another role or session. |
| Supervisor (`supervisor`) | Monitor fleet health and alerts, perform authorized alert triage/acknowledgement, inspect drift and propose configuration/change requests for review. | Cannot deploy configuration, approve privileged changes, enroll nodes or administer accounts, roles, credentials or trust. |
| Read-only (`read-only`) | View authorized inventory, alerts, configuration with secrets redacted, indicators and permitted reports/exports. | No triage writes, drafts, configuration changes, approvals or administration. Export access still requires explicit field/scope permission. |
| Approver (`approver`) | Inspect exact plans, diffs, validation and recovery evidence; approve or reject eligible requests with fresh strong authentication. | Cannot edit the request being approved, execute deployment, change configuration directly or administer identities. Critical approval requires a different principal from the initiator. |

Default-deny API grants must implement this matrix on both browser endpoints and the separate response boundary. The approver approves the immutable revision/target-bound plan; an administrator then executes within that approval's scope and expiry. Automatic validation still precedes every change. A policy may require independent approval for additional ordinary operations, but must not relax the mandatory critical-change boundary. Alert acknowledgement changes workflow metadata, never the firewall decision or source-owned ban.

Role assignment, reassignment, multiple sessions and any permitted combination of roles must not bypass separation of duties. Role or scope revocation invalidates affected pending work and sessions according to the existing authorization contract. Protect role changes through the existing privileged identity workflow; no self-escalation or default shared administrator.

- [ ] Tests implement all four roles across views, streams, exports, triage, TOML drafts, validation, approval, deployment, rollback and enrollment/account management; every disallowed operation is rejected server-side.
- [ ] Scope revocation and role changes invalidate stale grants; multi-role assignments, separate sessions and alternate credentials of the same principal cannot self-approve critical work.

## Named accounts, MFA and account recovery

Owner requirement recorded on October 12, 2026: support named usernames, passwords, OTP, passkeys and hardware security keys such as compatible YubiKey devices. RBAC defines permitted operations and node scope after authentication; it is not an authentication mechanism. These requirements are planned, not implemented.

- Preserve OIDC as the preferred enterprise integration. The enterprise IdP can provide passwords, TOTP and WebAuthn authentication without copying passwords or OTP seeds into the console. Bind identities to stable issuer/subject pairs, not mutable display names or email alone. Validate provider-specific assurance mappings, authentication time and required step-up; a generic `mfa` claim alone does not prove phishing resistance. Step-up failure or IdP outage must not silently select a weaker login path.
- Also design an explicitly enabled standalone identity profile for internal deployments without an IdP. It must support the same named-account and factor lifecycle using maintained libraries and reviewed standards, not a home-grown protocol. Local and federated account namespaces must remain distinct, with no automatic linking by username/email and no default or shared administrator password. Freeze the profile and its resource budgets in the ADR before implementation. Do not require a paid identity service.
- Provide password plus time-based OTP (TOTP) for roles whose explicit policy permits it. Use bounded password-hashing cost and login concurrency, salted memory-hard password hashes, password-manager support and compromised-password screening using an offline-capable policy. Protect OTP seeds at rest with separately controlled key material, restrict enrollment display, reject OTP reuse and rate-limit verification. Never log credentials, seeds, recovery codes or authentication assertions. OTP is not phishing-resistant and is not an equivalent fallback for privileged access.
- Provide WebAuthn passkeys and FIDO2 security keys, including compatible YubiKey devices. Require user verification for privileged authentication, such as the authenticator PIN or local biometric, in addition to possession. Verify challenge freshness and single use, exact allowed origin/RP ID, credential/account binding and ceremony type with a maintained verifier. Use enterprise-controlled DNS and trusted HTTPS certificates; internal deployment does not permit insecure origins or TLS bypass. YubiKey denotes a device family, not a separate factor to stack on top of the same passkey. Legacy Yubico OTP is not a substitute for the required FIDO2 mode.
- Require phishing-resistant authentication for supervisor, approver and administrator permissions and for sensitive exports/enrollment/credential or role changes. A user-verified passkey can provide a passwordless path; do not require password, OTP, passkey and YubiKey at every login or count one device twice. Support an explicit policy for device-bound versus synchronized passkeys; synchronized credentials do not establish non-exportable hardware assurance. Higher-assurance deployments can require approved device-bound credentials. Review attestation/privacy and available authenticator metadata rather than infer assurance from a product name.
- Offer a scoped security settings screen to enroll, name, inspect and revoke factors and sessions, with recent strong reauthentication for changes. Encourage two independently held authenticators for privileged accounts. Lost-device recovery must be separately authorized, audited, time-bounded and unable to grant privileged access directly through TOTP, email, SMS or a recovery code. If recovery codes are offered for an eligible role, generate high-entropy single-use values, store only protected verifiers and consume them atomically. Privileged recovery must revoke affected sessions/factors and re-establish a phishing-resistant authenticator before privileged operations resume. Define a separately reviewed, disabled-by-default emergency-access procedure without permanent MFA bypass.
- Keep authentication controls independent of agent mTLS, evidence signing and BunkerWeb synchronization credentials. Dashboard login, MFA recovery and IdP availability must never become prerequisites for existing automatic BunkerWeb exchanges or local protection.

Acceptance additions:

- [ ] Both federated and explicitly enabled standalone identity profiles pass named-account, lifecycle, role/scope isolation and no-default-credentials tests. Disabled profiles expose no alternate authentication path.
- [ ] Password/TOTP, user-verified passkeys and compatible FIDO2 hardware keys pass enrollment/login/revocation tests; privileged operations reject OTP-only assurance, missing user verification, stale step-up and downgrade attempts.
- [ ] Verification rejects wrong origins/RP IDs, replayed challenges/OTPs, substituted accounts, malformed assertions and invalid OIDC assurance mappings. Synchronized passkeys and zero/nonmonotonic signature counters follow the reviewed authenticator policy rather than an invented hardware guarantee.
- [ ] Lost authenticators, concurrent recovery-code use, credential replacement, role changes, session revocation and IdP outages preserve the privileged MFA boundary. All sensitive flows are audited without secrets.
- [ ] Authentication and recovery screens use the official SysWarden identity, accessible keyboard workflows and explicit failure states. Bounded hashing and login flood tests fit the lightweight console budget on existing resources.

Design references: [NIST SP 800-63B-4 authentication and authenticator management](https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-4/sp800-63b.html), [W3C Web Authentication](https://www.w3.org/TR/webauthn-3/). These references guide the ADR and tests; they do not establish compliance or certification.

## Official visual identity and shared semantics

- Use https://syswarden.io/ as the brand reference. Reuse the exact official logo asset and wordmark, Outfit and Fira Code fonts, light/dark palettes, typography hierarchy, spacing and border conventions. Pin the reviewed asset revision and its checksums; bundle fonts and assets locally. Do not redraw the logo or depend on the public website at runtime.
- Capture approved design tokens and reusable web components: navigation, cards, tables, charts, map legend, filters, forms, badges, focus rings, confirmations and detail panels. Review all loading, empty, stale, partial, denied, disconnected and failed states. Dense operational layouts must retain the site's identity and readable contrast.
- Coordinate with #234 and #255 on vocabulary, event identity, layer mapping, severity, source context and navigation. Share schemas and authoritative semantics, not a terminal renderer embedded in a browser. Observation, policy decision, historical enforcement outcome and current control state remain separate.
- Support actual L2-L7 telemetry, including non-IP observations and unsupported/unknown classifications. Known, protected or previously seen sources may still require investigation. A no-match reputation lookup is not proof of safety, and missing telemetry is not an empty healthy feed.
- Target WCAG 2.2 AA with keyboard operation, visible focus, reduced motion, accessible names, zoom/reflow and equivalent text/table views for visualizations. Use icons and labels alongside color. Test representative desktop, tablet and narrow browser layouts without creating a separate native mobile application.

## Screens and navigation

| Screen | Required operator workflow |
| --- | --- |
| Fleet overview | Rate-based KPI cards, percentage trends, coverage/freshness indicators and drill-downs. Show active node scope, time window and data-quality limitations. |
| Fleet inventory | Searchable, sortable, paginated server table with stable node identity, labels/site, authorized IPv4/IPv6 addresses, version, last contact, policy status and independently verified protection state. Saved views must respect current permissions. |
| External | Internet-exposed servers with the 2D world map, linked inventory, authorized addresses, exposure provenance and separate protection/health state. An exposed on-premises server belongs here and retains its hosting label. |
| Internal | Internal-only servers, including on-premises deployments, organized in an accessible inventory by approved site and network segment. No world map or IP-geolocation requirement for this tab. |
| Server detail | Identity and enrollment state, reachability, clock/freshness, current policy and verified controls, relevant supported alerts, version, approved action history and evidence. Reachability is not proof of protection. |
| BunkerWeb | Contextual integration view for authorized participating servers: health, supported capabilities, associated alerts, source-owned temporary claims, expiry and applicable HA state. Preserve visibility when a known integration becomes stale or unavailable. |
| Live alerts and incidents | Shared #255 semantics, supported L2-L7 filters, primary L4/L7 triage, stable selection, pause-display/resume, replay boundaries and #228 incident drill-down. Preserve node/time/filter context on return. |
| Configuration | Scoped per-node/group TOML editing, schema and semantic validation, redacted diffs, independent critical approval, canary/wave rollout, drift detection and verified rollback. |
| Policy and response | Typed policy templates and bounded rollout plans, target preview, diff, approval, expiry, progress, per-node verification and rollback through #230. Never provide arbitrary shell or raw firewall input. |
| Indicators and reports | Documented percentage KPIs, comparable periods, trends, accessible pie/donut charts and controlled exports. Expose formulas, coverage and evidence quality. |
| Access, enrollment and audit | Scoped membership and role management, certificate lifecycle, retention, console health, export jobs and immutable action history, with appropriate separation of duties. |

Use explicit, reversible navigation with breadcrumbs and stable identifiers. Preserve supported scope and filters across cards, charts, the map, tables, alerts and details. Disclose unsupported filters rather than silently broadening a query. Share links must not bypass authorization or expose sensitive values in URLs.

## External and Internal fleet navigation

Owner requirement recorded on October 13, 2026: provide distinct **External** and **Internal** tabs. Keep the management console itself internal in both cases; an External fleet tab never authorizes an Internet-facing console.

- **External:** show servers with an explicitly established Internet exposure, regardless of where they are hosted. The 2D world map belongs to this tab and uses only its authorized fleet population. Keep the linked table usable when a node has no approved location. An exposed on-premises server remains in External with an `On-premises` hosting label.
- **Internal:** show servers explicitly classified as internal-only, with the on-premises fleet as the primary workflow. Use a searchable table grouped by approved site/network segment, with private addresses, health, protection state and alerts subject to field permissions. Private cloud hosting may also be internal-only; retain its actual hosting label. Do not require a world map or geolocation in this view.
- Keep `exposure` and `hosting_model` as separate authoritative inventory attributes. Hosting labels such as on-premises, cloud or colocation do not prove exposure. A public IP does not prove an open service, and a private IP does not exclude exposure through NAT, a load balancer or a reverse proxy. Do not perform unsolicited active scans to populate this classification.
- Record the classification source, verification time and freshness from administrator-approved inventory/configuration and supported evidence. Distinguish Internet-exposed, internal-only and unknown/unverified exposure. Unknown or stale classification must remain visibly available in the global inventory and a `Needs classification` filter; never silently assign it to Internal or portray it as protected. Preserve last-known information with its uncertainty.
- A mixed-use server with an established Internet-facing path appears once in External. Retain its internal/management endpoints as separately labeled, permission-filtered fields. Tabs are views of stable enrolled identities, not duplicate enrollments or independent control planes. Reclassification must preserve alert history, evidence, deep-link context and existing ownership.
- Carry the selected exposure scope through inventory, server details, supported alerts, the contextual BunkerWeb tab, rate indicators and exports. Apply authorization before filtering, aggregation, map serialization and caching. Switching tabs does not change roles or grant access to another population.
- Keep headline KPIs in rates. Show the exact classified population, eligible denominator, classification freshness and unknown coverage. Do not let missing classification improve a security rate or count one node in both tab populations. Global coverage and scoped formulas must reconcile to the same snapshot.
- Include permitted exposure/hosting labels, provenance, freshness and the selected tab/filter in exports. Exposure changes cannot silently alter a previously approved response plan: preserve exact target binding and recheck the existing action preconditions.

These are planning requirements, not an implemented discovery engine or a completed UI.

## Dedicated BunkerWeb integration tab

Owner decision recorded on October 12, 2026: provide a dedicated **BunkerWeb** tab when an authorized server uses the integration. Determine participation from authoritative configuration and established integration state, not an untrusted event label. Scope the tab to the selected authorized fleet or server.

- Distinguish verified log collection, scheduler synchronization and combined operation. A log-only integration may warrant the tab while optional synchronization stays disabled. A path or source label alone is not proof of a partner deployment; displaying the tab must never enable synchronization.
- Show participating servers, enablement, last successful exchange, synchronization health/errors, observed API/plugin version only when attested, supported capabilities, and applicable writer/standby and fence state. Missing evidence stays unknown.
- Keep a known integration visible when unreachable, stale or failed. Preserve authorized history with an explicit disabled state after intentional deactivation. Do not hide an outage by making the tab disappear.
- Provide associated alerts and temporary-ban claim details, including authenticated source scope, available timestamps, TTL/expiry, requested versus verified outcome and current control evidence. A withdrawn partner claim does not imply a globally unblocked IP when another owner still protects it.
- Use the same percentage KPI catalog, explicit populations, freshness and unavailable-denominator rules as other dashboard views. Apply node and field authorization before tables, aggregates, streams or exports are generated.
- Preserve the existing BunkerWeb synchronization API, authentication, source ownership, bounded TTL, retry/withdrawal semantics, log collection and HA restrictions. Automatic plugin exchanges remain independent of the dashboard and its browser sessions. Do not add interactive approval to every existing plugin request or require the plugin to call through the console.
- Keep browsing read-only. Any supported human-initiated action uses #230/#232 with exact authorization, scope, verification and audit. The tab must not expose integration secrets, embed a general partner administrator session, or become a new arbitrary proxy.
- Use SysWarden's official visual components and preserve scope, time window and selection between the tab, fleet table, alerts and evidence. This view supplements the integration without replacing BunkerWeb's own administration interface.

## KPI contract: rates, never raw-count KPIs

**All headline and report KPIs must be rates, primarily percentages. Do not present totals of servers, alerts, blocked addresses or incidents as KPI cards.** Operational entity rows and explicitly authorized calculation provenance may contain quantities; they must not become substitute count-based KPIs.

Maintain a versioned indicator catalog with definition, numerator, denominator, eligible population, inclusions/exclusions, time window, freshness, unit, precision, aggregation method and evidence source. Distinguish a node-state snapshot from a rate over events or actions during an interval.

| Initial indicator | Required definition |
| --- | --- |
| Reporting coverage | Eligible enrolled nodes with a timely valid report / all eligible enrolled nodes in scope. |
| Verified protection coverage | Intended protected nodes with current evidence of the required enforcement state / all nodes intended to be protected in scope. Unknown or stale evidence cannot count as verified. |
| Policy conformity | Eligible managed nodes with current attestation of conformity / all eligible managed nodes in scope. |
| Telemetry freshness compliance | Eligible source observations meeting the declared freshness requirement / all expected eligible source observations for the measured interval. Document missing observations. |
| Verified response success | Unique eligible transactions with a verified successful result / all eligible transactions whose verification deadline falls in the interval. Distinguish pending, failed, expired and unknown outcomes; retries cannot inflate either side. |
| Alert distribution | Each mutually exclusive severity or outcome category / all eligible retained observations in the same authorized snapshot and interval. Use separate charts for different dimensions. |

- Aggregate compatible populations by summing eligible numerators and denominators, not averaging server or group percentages. Deduplicate overlapping groups and stable event/transaction identities. Do not merge incompatible formula versions.
- A missing or zero denominator yields `Not available`, never a fabricated 0% or 100%. Show coverage and unknown/stale shares. Exclusions must be explicit and reviewable; dropping unreachable nodes must not improve the displayed protection rate.
- Do not invent a percentage of all attacks blocked without an observable eligible denominator, a false-positive rate without adjudicated reference data, or a security/risk score disguised as a measured rate.
- Every pie/donut represents mutually exclusive parts of one defined population, including unknown when applicable. Overlapping detections must not appear as exclusive slices. Explain rounding, incomplete acquisition and insufficient samples. Provide an equivalent accessible table and a drill-down into the same snapshot.
- UI, charts and exports must use identical formula versions, scope and snapshots. Comparison periods must disclose changed membership, coverage or policy definitions. User-selected display time zones must not change the underlying interval semantics.

## External 2D world map: fleet geography, IP addresses and state

- Limit the world map to the authorized External population. Provide an interactive, lightweight 2D vector world map, with pan, bounded zoom, reset, a clear legend and selection linked to the server table. Use a bundled, simplified, versioned basemap, such as reviewed Natural Earth data, with recorded provenance and license. No mandatory external tile server, map API key, WebGL/3D globe or runtime tracking.
- Prefer administrator-approved site metadata or an explicitly configured asset inventory for location. Optional IP geolocation uses a locally hosted, licensed database with a visible source, revision and freshness. Never transmit inventory addresses to an external geolocation service by default.
- A marker identifies the enrolled server, not an attacker. Its detail panel shows the authorized node name, site/country/region, permitted IP addresses, last successful contact and separate reachability, protection, policy and alert states. Label management, private, public and advertised endpoint addresses distinctly; an IP is not the node's stable identity.
- Label location provenance and precision. An IP-derived country, approximate point or NAT egress location is not proof of a machine's physical location. Private, reserved, unmapped and location-redacted addresses remain visible in a dedicated inventory group without fabricated coordinates. Never substitute `(0, 0)` for missing location. Validate coordinates and support IPv4/IPv6 and multiple addresses per node.
- Overlapping nodes must remain individually inspectable through clustering or site expansion. Cluster summaries show state proportions and unknown/stale status, not a reassuring green average that hides a degraded member. Use the same rate catalog and authorized population as the fleet overview.
- Filters for site/region, node group, version, policy, reachability, protection and alert severity must synchronize with the table. Clearly separate `Unreachable`, `Stale`, `Protection degraded`, `Policy drift`, `Pending enrollment` and `State unknown`; connection loss alone does not prove enforcement stopped.
- Apply node and field permissions before serialization. Unauthorized nodes, IP addresses, site labels and coordinates must be absent from map payloads, aggregates, tooltips, search, caches and exports. Support coarse location and IP masking where policy requires it. No automatic browser geolocation request.
- Provide complete keyboard and screen-reader access through an equivalent table and details view. The map is an additional view, never the only way to locate a server or take an approved action. A map selection cannot trigger a mutation.

## Approved administration and blast-radius control

Use #230 and #232 for all remote changes: authenticated authority, exact preview, preconditions, scope, TTL, approval, durable commit, post-verification, evidence and supported rollback. Finalize the supported typed operation catalog with #231 before implementation. Policy changes, de-enrollment and other disruptive actions must have explicit recovery behavior.

Resolve groups into an immutable, exact target list before approval, bind its digest and policy revision to the plan, and reject changes after approval. Support bounded canary waves, concurrency limits, stop conditions and per-node outcomes. Partial success must remain explicit; do not imply fleet-wide atomicity. Reconnects and retries must be idempotent, and stale queued actions must expire. Preserve administrator access and unrelated protections. Do not store a general-purpose fleet root key or expose a web shell.

## Exports and evidence

- Provide versioned CSV and JSON indicator exports, a safe spreadsheet export and a print-ready report suitable for PDF. Keep the runtime lightweight; a mandatory headless browser service is not required for print/PDF. All KPI values remain rates, consistent with the screen.
- Attach authorized scope, filters, time window, formula/schema versions, snapshot identity, generation time, freshness, coverage and limitations. Numerator/denominator provenance may be included in a clearly labeled calculation appendix subject to the same permissions. Do not export credentials or raw sensitive event payloads by default.
- Authorize export creation and download independently against current rights. Use bounded jobs, size and concurrency quotas, cancellation, retention and expiry. Prevent cross-user cache leakage. Protect CSV formula injection and spreadsheet cells, with no untrusted formulas, macros or external relationships. Report rendering must not fetch untrusted remote resources.
- Record export activity and bind integrity manifests or existing signed evidence capsules through #232 when a verifiable report is requested. Evidence keys stay separate from release keys and browser sessions. A screenshot or plain CSV must never be described as cryptographically verified evidence.

## Fleet configuration management through TOML

Owner requirement recorded on October 21, 2026: dashboard administrators with the appropriate node-group grants must be able to propose, validate, approve and deploy SysWarden configuration changes to individual nodes, selected groups or the authorized fleet. This is an explicit v5.00.0 deliverable, not an implemented editor. Coordinate the typed operation catalog and durable execution with #230, #231 and #232, authenticated node membership with #233, and migration/access preservation with #235, #337 and #422.

- Add a **Configuration** workflow to the fleet and server views: current declared configuration, supported effective values, configuration revision, management ownership, local overrides, drift and freshness. Provide typed forms and an advanced TOML view of the same supported schema, plus semantic and file-level change previews. Bind the UI to the selected nodes' actual product/schema versions and capabilities; unsupported or mixed-version fields must be explicit. Do not silently flatten group templates over node-specific or administrator-managed values.
- Separate scoped configuration read, edit, approve, apply and rollback permissions. A dashboard administrator account does not imply unrestricted node scope, host root access or approval of every operation. Enforce permissions and current strong authentication on the server and recheck authority before execution. Critical changes, including SSH access, firewall reachability, trust, credentials and disruptive module changes, require a different authorized approver under the existing separation-of-duties policy. Configuration browsing and previews never change a node.
- Parse TOML and validate types, supported keys, limits, cross-module dependencies and security semantics centrally and again on the target node. Reject malformed, duplicate/ambiguous or unsupported entries; do not accept arbitrary paths, Include targets, commands, hooks or raw firewall instructions. Render an explicit validation report and a plan of configuration writes, module transitions and required reloads/restarts before approval. A syntactically valid TOML document alone is not a safe change.
- Bind approval to exact staged content, expected current configuration revisions, enrolled node identities/epochs, resolved target-list digest, allowed operations, expiry and recovery policy. Concurrent local edits, external automation, changed membership/capability or an expired approval invalidate the affected plan; never overwrite them or silently rebase an approved change. Administrator/Ansible-owned inputs require an explicit ownership decision, not takeover based on a filename or the dashboard role.
- Store only bounded typed jobs and use the existing authenticated outbound node channel and independent response authority. Enrollment/mTLS proves channel identity, not permission to alter configuration. Apply through the local ownership-aware configuration transaction with protected staging, durable evidence and atomic file replacement where supported. Preserve unrelated fields, comments, permissions, labels and administrator protections. Cross-file or cross-node operations must expose partial outcomes rather than claiming unsupported atomicity. There is no generic remote file editor or shell.
- Deploy a canary first, then bounded waves with concurrency limits, pause/cancel controls and stop conditions. Revalidate each node before a wave. Show separate proposed, validated, approved, persisted, applied, runtime-verified, failed, expired, rolled-back and unreachable states. An accepted job or a saved file is not verified enforcement. Reconnect/retry must be idempotent; disconnected nodes cannot receive stale instructions or appear successful.
- Define supported rollback in the approved plan and retain protected prior configuration and evidence. Rollback must preserve later administrator edits, configuration ownership and local security boundaries. Automatic rollback is permitted only for explicitly approved, still-valid safe inverse operations; otherwise stop and present a bounded recovery path. Verify restored runtime behavior and independent administrator access for affected SSH/network changes. The dedicated SSH transaction and fresh access checks remain mandatory.
- Never return secret values, private keys, OTP seeds or integration credentials to the TOML editor, previews, exports, logs or browser storage. Use redacted placeholders and separately authorized secret references/provisioning; a placeholder must not overwrite a real secret. Bind references/revisions into the approved plan without disclosing their values. Audit the actor, approver, target scope, redacted diff, revisions, time and per-node verified outcome with the existing protected evidence contract.
- Preserve #422: fresh native packages remain standard-list-only. Dashboard availability, enrollment or template assignment must not silently enable SSH/CIS/OS hardening or optional modules. Each supported module change needs explicit TOML selection and the corresponding validated transition. Upgrades preserve administrator configuration and existing protection. Console/IdP/network outages preserve local enforcement, and BunkerWeb's automatic source ownership, expiry and HA exchanges remain independent.

Acceptance additions for this workflow:

- [ ] An authorized administrator completes a single-node and scoped fleet edit through draft, TOML/schema/semantic validation, exact diff, approval, canary, waves and independently verified per-node outcomes; the UI follows the official design tokens and keyboard/accessibility rules.
- [ ] Read-only, wrong-group, revoked and insufficient-assurance accounts cannot edit/apply; self-approval of a critical change, modified targets/payloads and stale approvals are rejected at both console and node boundaries.
- [ ] Fixtures cover malformed/duplicate TOML keys, unknown fields, mixed versions, conflicting templates/local overrides, stale reads, concurrent administrator/Ansible edits, partial multi-file failure and preserved unrelated configuration/metadata.
- [ ] Crash/restart, lost acknowledgements, offline nodes, replay, retry, cancellation, failed canaries and partial fleet failure preserve truthful outcomes and pass the approved rollback/recovery contract without overwriting later administrator work.
- [ ] Secrets remain absent from browser responses, previews, audit payloads and exports; redacted fields do not replace stored credentials. Read-only access and previews cause no configuration or runtime mutation.
- [ ] Fresh native installations remain minimal; explicit SSH/CIS/optional-module changes use their respective lifecycle gates. SSH/network changes preserve fresh administrator access, and BunkerWeb continues independently during dashboard outage and rollback. Capacity tests use the existing 500-agent simulation target and existing machines only.

## Lightweight operation and failure budgets

The 500-server figure is a logical capacity target to test by simulating 500 independently identified agents on existing hardware. It does not require owning, renting or provisioning 500 real servers. This is a test target, not a current capacity guarantee. Freeze the simulated workload with #223 before implementation: active viewers, health cadence, average and burst event rates, payload sizes, replay window, retention, map density and export concurrency.

Perform functional and native IVV with real agents on the existing laboratory machines, within the applicable authorization for each campaign. Use synthetic agents and events for the larger capacity, concurrency and failure scenarios. Record which evidence comes from simulation and which comes from real systems; simulation does not establish end-to-end operation on 500 physical hosts. Bound the load generator's own CPU, RAM and storage, measure it separately from the console, and disclose shared-host contention and simulation limitations.

Resource budgets mean CPU, RAM, storage, network and latency limits, not a financial allocation. Implement and validate this work package using existing resources, without additional spending: no additional server rental, hardware purchase, paid service, license or other chargeable test resource. The reference console VM below is a resource allocation on existing capacity, not a purchase requirement. If the available resources cannot support a planned test, document the limitation and revisit the test design; do not provision paid infrastructure or claim an unperformed test passed.

Proposed starting targets for that agreed profile are a 2-vCPU/2-GiB console VM, steady service RSS at most 512 MiB, bounded burst RSS at most 1 GiB, p95 cached read API latency at most 250 ms and p95 receipt-to-visible alert latency at most 2 seconds under nominal load. Measure acquisition cadence and remote delay separately. Target at most 200 KiB compressed initial JavaScript; lazy-load the bounded map dataset and avoid unbounded DOM growth. Review these targets before freezing them; record any change and its rationale rather than silently raising a failing limit.

Measure added agent CPU, memory, network and disk overhead against the accepted standalone baseline and the #223 regression boundary. Exercise at least an eight-hour mixed-view soak, event bursts, many disconnected nodes, certificate rotation, slow clients, disk pressure, restart and restore. Document caps and visible overload behavior. Define RPO/RTO for the single-active profile and verify recovery; do not claim high availability without a separately accepted design and failure evidence.

## Acceptance criteria and IVV evidence

- [ ] The ADR, data flows, threat model, operation catalog, deployment profile and resource budgets are reviewed with #223. Read authority, response authority and compromised-node boundaries are explicit.
- [ ] Reviewed synthetic mockups and visual regression fixtures demonstrate the official logo, fonts and design tokens across every screen, light/dark themes and failure states. No private infrastructure or operational evidence appears in public examples.
- [ ] The fleet table, map, cards, charts, alerts and detail navigation preserve authorized scope, supported filters and stable selection. Representative operator workflows pass keyboard and accessibility review against WCAG 2.2 AA.
- [ ] External/Internal fixtures cover an exposed cloud server, internal-only on-premises server, exposed on-premises server, private cloud server, private-address service exposed through a proxy/NAT path, mixed endpoints, unknown/stale classification and reclassification. No IP/hosting heuristic invents exposure; stable nodes are not duplicated or lost.
- [ ] Only External renders the world map. Internal supports complete site/segment table workflows. Keyboard navigation, scope switching, alerts, BunkerWeb context, percentage denominators, global classification coverage and exports reconcile to the same authorized snapshot; revoked scope never survives in map/table caches.
- [ ] Rate fixtures cover unequal group sizes, overlapping groups, missing/zero denominators, stale nodes, incomplete streams, duplicates, pending actions, precision and formula changes. No headline KPI or exported KPI is silently replaced by a count; UI and exports reconcile to the same snapshot.
- [ ] Map IVV covers approved and approximate locations, IPv4/IPv6, private/unmapped addresses, multiple addresses, overlapping markers, redaction, invalid coordinates and unknown state. It remains usable without public Internet access and without leaking IP/location data to external services.
- [ ] Shared #224/#234/#255 fixtures demonstrate consistent L2-L7 alert semantics, independent source context, authoritative verdicts, freshness, evidence gaps and current versus historical enforcement state.
- [ ] The BunkerWeb tab passes configured/disabled/stale/unreachable/unauthorized states, overlapping owners, TTL/expiry and HA standby fixtures. Existing authenticated plugin API and log-ingestion regressions pass; real partner IVV remains separately identified. Dashboard/IdP outages do not interrupt existing automatic integration exchanges, and read-only views cannot reload or mutate the partner stack.
- [ ] Authentication and authorization tests cover session theft boundaries, CSRF, XSS, IDOR, cross-group leakage, malicious node metadata, stream replay, revocation, enrollment, certificate rotation and unauthorized exports. Map and aggregate queries are explicitly included.
- [ ] Applicable OWASP ASVS 5.0 requirements are mapped and verified, using Level 2 as the minimum web application baseline with additional reviewed controls for privileged fleet operations. An independent security review and scoped penetration test address the actual deployment and response threat model. No unsupported certification claim is made.
- [ ] Every delivered write operation passes preview/approval, immutable-target, canary, expiry, retry, partial-failure, verification, access-preservation and rollback tests through #230/#232. Read-only browsing cannot mutate policy or firewall state.
- [ ] Loss of the console, IdP or fleet connection preserves local protection. Restart and restore do not replay expired actions, revive revoked identities or erase mandatory audit history. Disk-pressure and recovery scenarios pass the frozen RPO/RTO contract.
- [ ] A simulation of 500 independently identified agents, the eight-hour soak and burst/slow-client/export scenarios meet frozen resource and latency budgets on existing hardware. Functional and native IVV passes on the existing laboratory machines. Evidence distinguishes simulated capacity from real-agent validation, records generator overhead and limitations, and confirms that the campaign used no additional paid resources. Publish bounded capacities and measured limitations, not inferred scalability.
- [ ] Exports pass formula-injection, redaction, authorization, revocation, integrity, consistency and resource-limit checks. CSV/JSON, spreadsheet and printable reports use the rate catalog and preserve evidence-quality caveats.
- [ ] Signed native delivery, SBOM/provenance, upgrade, rollback and independent uninstall/remove/purge paths pass for the supported console matrix. Removal preserves administrator configuration and enrolled-node protection; retention of private evidence/backups is explicit.
- [ ] English guidance at https://syswarden.io/docs/ covers deployment, enrollment, IdP/RBAC, map/geolocation privacy, rate formulas, approved operations, exports, limits, backup/restore and removal. Keep README concise and link to the canonical guidance. Publish release claims only after acceptance.

## Dependencies and scope ownership

- #222 and #223: roadmap inclusion, threat model, scope and resource budgets.
- #224 and #225: versioned authoritative schemas and bounded durable journal.
- #228: incident and timeline semantics.
- #230, #231 and #232: typed approved response, bounded playbooks and signed evidence.
- #233: explicit authenticated fleet membership and read-plane contracts. Extend this contract rather than creating a competing trust plane.
- #234 and #255: coordinated TUI and real-time L2-L7 alert semantics. This issue owns the web shell, fleet map, web authorization, percentage KPI catalog and web reports; it does not replace the terminal work packages.
- #235 and #236: migration, operator documentation, native acceptance and signed release integration.

Non-goals: public SaaS/multi-tenant hosting, an Internet-facing management console, arbitrary remote shell, autonomous policy decisions, mandatory third-party map/identity/analytics services, or fleet orchestration outside the reviewed bounded operation catalog. An enterprise IdP is operator-selected and may be hosted internally.

## Primary design references

- [SysWarden official visual identity](https://syswarden.io/)
- [NIST SP 800-207: Zero Trust Architecture](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/207/final)
- [OpenID Connect Core](https://openid.net/specs/openid-connect-core-1_0.html) and [OAuth security best current practice, RFC 9700](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9700/)
- [OWASP ASVS](https://owasp.org/projects/asvs) and [session management guidance](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Session_Management_Cheat_Sheet.html)
- [Go html/template](https://pkg.go.dev/html/template), [HTML server-sent events](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/server-sent-events.html) and [SQLite WAL constraints](https://sqlite.org/wal.html)
- [WCAG 2.2](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/)
- [Natural Earth basemap terms](https://www.naturalearthdata.com/about/terms-of-use/)

Link accepted designs, implementation PRs, IVV evidence and operator guidance here. Close only when the scoped deliverables and acceptance criteria are reviewed and accepted. This planning issue does not alter the current stable v4 release.

## Explicit node enrollment coordination

Planning clarification recorded on October 14, 2026: #233 now records the proposed
bootstrap and certificate lifecycle for this dashboard. Its existing outbound
mTLS model is retained. The proposed initial admission uses one short-lived,
single-use invitation per node, local key generation, key-possession proof and
independent approval binding the exact node/key/scope before certificate issuance.
The detailed profile remains subject to the reviewed ADR before implementation.

Use #233 as the single enrollment protocol owner. Dashboard workflows must show
pending/approved/revoked state and authorized public fingerprints, enforce scoped
strongly authenticated approval and audit, and never expose node keys or bootstrap
secrets to the browser. Cover live-session revocation, rotation, loss/restore,
replay and concurrent redemption through shared WP11/WP18 fixtures. A transport
identity never grants privileged response authority. Local protection and the
independent BunkerWeb contract remain available without this dashboard or PKI.

- [ ] WP11/WP18 ADR and shared fixtures cover the complete #233 admission,
  renewal, revocation and recovery lifecycle before enrollment UI acceptance.

This is planning detail, not a delivered enrollment service or a closed criterion.
